atoms.title: The neuron doctrine
atoms.summary: The nervous system is built from discrete cells — neurons — that are not continuous with one another, but signal across gaps.

depths.eli5: Your brain is made of cells. A long time ago, people argued about whether those cells were all joined into one big continuous mesh (like a fishing net with no gaps) or were separate little units. The neuron doctrine is the winning answer: the brain is built from separate cells called neurons, each its own closed bag with its own outer skin (its membrane). They are not fused together — they sit next to each other and pass signals across tiny gaps, the way people pass notes hand to hand instead of being wired into one circuit. A 'neuron' is just the name for one of these signaling cells.
depths.core: The older 'reticular theory' held that the nervous system was one continuous web of fused fibers. Using tissue stained by the Golgi method (a silver stain that randomly blackens a few whole cells so their full shape stands out), Santiago Ramón y Cajal argued the opposite: neurons are individual cells, each bounded by its own membrane (the cell's outer skin). The doctrine has four claims: (1) the neuron is the basic structural and functional unit of the nervous system; (2) neurons are discrete cells, not physically fused; (3) within a neuron, signals normally flow one direction — from the dendrites (input branches) and soma (cell body) toward the axon (the output cable) and its terminals (the output tips); and (4) connections are specific and orderly, not random. This one-way-flow claim is called 'dynamic polarization.'
depths.deep: Cajal could not see the synaptic cleft (the gap between two neurons) directly — it is about 20 nanometers wide, far smaller than a light microscope can resolve (a nanometer is a billionth of a meter; visible light can only resolve features a few hundred nanometers across). So the doctrine was an inference from the shape of stained cells and the direction in which growing nerve tips (growth cones) extended, not a direct observation. It was only confirmed directly in the 1950s by the electron microscope, which uses electrons instead of light and can resolve such gaps. The dynamic-polarization principle — that signals run one way — is what makes a brain a computing device (with inputs, processing, and outputs) rather than a passive wire that conducts in any direction.

atoms.note: Cajal vs Golgi: they shared the 1906 Nobel Prize while still disagreeing — Golgi's own staining method, used by Cajal, is what defeated Golgi's reticular theory.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Before you can talk about how a brain computes, you have to know what it is *made of*. A **neuron** is a single cell specialized for signaling — a tiny living unit, bounded by its own **membrane** (the thin oily skin that separates inside from outside). Around 1900 there was a real fight about how these cells were arranged. One camp (the *reticular theory*) said the brain was one giant continuous mesh of fused fibers, like a fishnet with no breaks. The other camp said the brain is built from *separate* cells that merely sit next to each other and pass signals across gaps — the way people hand notes down a row rather than being soldered into one circuit. The winning answer is the **neuron doctrine**: the nervous system is built from discrete neurons.

### Precisely

The neuron doctrine makes four claims. **(1)** The neuron is the basic structural and functional unit of the nervous system. **(2)** Neurons are discrete cells, each enclosed by its own membrane, not physically continuous with their neighbors. **(3)** Signals flow in one preferred direction inside a neuron: from the **dendrites** (the branching input antennae) and the **soma** (cell body) toward the **axon** (the long output cable) and its terminals. This one-way rule is called **dynamic polarization**. **(4)** Connections are specific and orderly, not random.

### Worked example

Imagine staining a thin slice of brain with the **Golgi method** — a silver stain that, almost magically, blackens only a few cells out of thousands but blackens each chosen cell completely. Under the microscope you see a handful of fully drawn neurons standing alone against a clear background. Santiago Ramón y Cajal did exactly this and noticed that the inky black outline of one cell *stops* — there is a clear edge — and a separate cell begins nearby. He could not see the gap itself, but the abrupt ending of each cell's silhouette implied the cells were separate units, not one fused web.

### Why it's true / how it works

The decisive gap, the **synaptic cleft**, is only about $20\,\text{nm}$ wide ($1\,\text{nm} = 10^{-9}\,\text{m}$). Visible light cannot resolve features that small — the *diffraction limit* of a light microscope is a few hundred nanometers. So the doctrine began as an *inference* from cell shape and from the direction in which growing nerve tips (growth cones) extended, not a direct sighting. Direct confirmation came in the 1950s with the **electron microscope**, which uses electrons (far shorter wavelength than light) and could finally show the cleft as a real gap between two membranes.

### Where it connects

This is the foundation atom for everything else in this branch. The "input → soma → axon → output" picture of dynamic polarization sets up **neuron-structure** (the compartments) and ultimately the **action-potential** that travels one way down the axon. Discreteness is exactly what lets the **chemical-synapse** exist as a controllable relay — if cells were fused, there would be nothing to strengthen or weaken, and **hebbian-learning** would have no substrate.

### Watch out

The most common mistake is thinking the doctrine was *proved* by seeing the gap directly — it wasn't, for half a century. A second pitfall: the doctrine is *mostly* true, not absolutely. **Electrical synapses** (gap junctions) do let current flow directly between cells, a real exception. The doctrine is the right default, but biology kept one back door open.

atoms.title: Neuron structure & compartments
atoms.summary: A neuron is organized into dendrites (input), soma (integration), axon (transmission), and terminals (output), each with distinct molecular machinery.

depths.eli5: Picture a neuron as a tree with a long trunk. The leafy branches at the top (called dendrites) collect incoming messages from other neurons. Those messages flow down to the main body of the cell (the soma, just a fancy word for the cell body, where the nucleus lives). If enough messages arrive, the neuron fires a signal that shoots down the long trunk (the axon — a thin cable that can be very long, up to about a meter in your leg) all the way to the tips at the far end (the terminals), where it hands the message to the next neuron. Input at the top, output at the bottom.
depths.core: A neuron is divided into compartments, each with a different job. Dendrites receive synaptic inputs (signals arriving from other neurons at junctions called synapses) and funnel them toward the soma (cell body). The axon hillock — the spot where the axon leaves the soma — is the decision point: it adds up the inputs and triggers a 'spike' (a nerve signal, formally an action potential) if they are strong enough. The axon, often wrapped in a fatty insulation called myelin, carries that all-or-none spike (it either fires fully or not at all) down to the presynaptic terminals, where chemical messengers (neurotransmitters) are released onto the next cell. Each compartment carries its own specialized set of ion channels (protein pores that let charged particles cross the membrane) and receptors (proteins that detect chemical messengers).
depths.deep: This compartmentalization is functional, not just anatomical. The axon initial segment (the very start of the axon) has the highest concentration of voltage-gated sodium channels (Na⁺ channels that open in response to voltage) in the whole cell, which is exactly why it is the spike-initiation zone. Dendrites are instead dominated by receptors and slower channels suited to gradually combining inputs. The nodes of Ranvier — small bare gaps along a myelinated axon — pack sodium channels so the spike can leap between them. The neuron's geometry (how its dendrites branch, how thick its axon is) directly shapes how it combines inputs, so shape is part of computation.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Picture a neuron as a tree with one very long trunk. The leafy crown at the top — the **dendrites** — collects incoming messages from thousands of other neurons. Those messages flow down to the main body of the cell, the **soma** (just a fancy word for "cell body," where the nucleus lives). If enough of them arrive, the neuron fires a signal that shoots down the long trunk — the **axon**, a thin cable that can run up to about a meter — all the way to the tips at the far end, the **terminals**, where the message is handed to the next cell. Input at the top, output at the bottom.

### Precisely

A neuron is organized into **compartments**, each with distinct molecular machinery. **Dendrites** receive synaptic inputs and funnel the resulting voltage changes toward the soma. The **axon hillock** / **axon initial segment** — the spot where the axon leaves the soma — is the decision point: it sums the inputs and triggers a **spike** (action potential) if they exceed **threshold**. The **axon**, often sheathed in fatty **myelin**, carries that all-or-none spike to the **presynaptic terminals**, where **neurotransmitters** (chemical messengers) are released. Each compartment carries its own set of **ion channels** (protein pores that pass charged particles) and **receptors** (proteins that detect chemical messengers).

### Worked example

Suppose 1,000 synapses land on a cell's dendrites and each, by itself, raises the local voltage by a fraction of a millivolt. None alone matters. But the dendrites funnel these toward the axon initial segment, where they sum. If the running total at that one segment reaches the firing threshold (often around $-55\,\text{mV}$), a spike is launched — *only there*, because that segment has the highest density of voltage-gated sodium channels in the whole cell. Move the same summed voltage a few hundred micrometers into the dendrites and no spike would fire: the trigger zone is a specific place.

### Why it's true / how it works

Compartmentalization is *functional*, not merely anatomical. The **axon initial segment** packs the most voltage-gated $\text{Na}^+$ channels, which is exactly why it is the spike-initiation zone. Dendrites are instead dominated by receptors and slower channels suited to gradually combining inputs. The bare gaps along a myelinated axon — the **nodes of Ranvier** — also cluster $\text{Na}^+$ channels, letting the spike leap between them. So a neuron's geometry (how its dendrites branch, how thick its axon is) directly shapes how inputs combine: *shape is part of computation*.

### Where it connects

This atom unpacks claim (3) of **neuron-doctrine** (dynamic polarization) into physical parts. Dendritic geometry is the engine of **synaptic-integration**; the channel-rich initial segment is where the **action-potential** is born; myelin and nodes set up **saltatory-conduction**; the terminals are where the **chemical-synapse** does its work.

### Watch out

Don't picture every neuron as the textbook pyramidal cell. Some neurons have almost no dendrites, some have axons under a millimeter long, and a few signal without a conventional spike at all. The compartment *roles* (input, integrate, transmit, output) are the durable idea; the exact morphology varies enormously across cell types.

atoms.title: Ionic gradients & the Na⁺/K⁺ pump
atoms.summary: Active pumping maintains high K⁺ inside and high Na⁺ outside, storing the electrochemical energy every neural signal spends.

depths.eli5: Charged particles called ions float in and around every cell. Two of them matter here: sodium and potassium. A tiny machine in the cell's outer skin (a protein 'pump') constantly shoves sodium out of the cell and pulls potassium in. This leaves the inside and outside unequal — like separating two crowds — which stores energy, the same way pulling a slingshot back stores energy. Every nerve signal is that stored energy briefly being let go.
depths.core: An 'ion' is an atom carrying electric charge; sodium (written Na⁺) and potassium (K⁺) are the key ones here, both positively charged. The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase ('ATPase' means it burns ATP, the cell's energy currency) is a pump that swaps 3 sodium ions out of the cell for 2 potassium ions in, per ATP used — pushing each ion 'uphill' against its concentration gradient (from where it is scarce toward where it is already crowded). This builds an ionic imbalance: lots of potassium inside (~140 millimolar, a unit of concentration), lots of sodium outside (~145 mM). That imbalance is a stored reservoir of free energy (usable energy). Both the resting potential (the cell's steady idle voltage) and the action potential (the nerve spike) are controlled releases of this stored gradient.
depths.deep: The pump is electrogenic — each cycle moves a net of one positive charge out — so it adds a few millivolts (mV, thousandths of a volt) to the cell's voltage directly. But its main job is maintaining the concentration gradients that the Nernst and Goldman equations (covered next) use to compute the cell's voltage. Restoring these gradients after activity is a neuron's single largest energy cost, consuming roughly half the brain's entire energy budget. That is why neural signaling is, at bottom, an energy-management problem: the brain spends most of its fuel just keeping these batteries charged.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Every nerve signal is, at bottom, a controlled release of stored energy — and the store is a battery built from charged particles. An **ion** is an atom that carries electric charge. Two matter most here: sodium ($\text{Na}^+$) and potassium ($\text{K}^+$), both positive. A tiny protein machine in the membrane constantly shoves sodium *out* of the cell and drags potassium *in*. This leaves the inside and outside unequal — like separating two crowds, or pulling back a slingshot — and that imbalance *is* the stored energy that every spike spends.

### Precisely

The **$\text{Na}^+/\text{K}^+$-ATPase** ("ATPase" means it burns **ATP**, the cell's energy currency) is a pump that, per ATP consumed, ejects **3** $\text{Na}^+$ and imports **2** $\text{K}^+$, each pushed "uphill" against its concentration gradient. The result is a standing imbalance: potassium high inside ($\sim 140\,\text{mM}$, millimolar) and sodium high outside ($\sim 145\,\text{mM}$). This separation stores **free energy** that the **nernst** and **goldman** equations convert into a voltage.

### Worked example

Start with the gradients flat (equal concentrations inside and out) and switch the pump on. Each cycle costs one ATP and moves $3\,\text{Na}^+$ out for $2\,\text{K}^+$ in. After many cycles, potassium piles up inside and sodium piles up outside. Because $3$ positive charges leave but only $2$ enter per cycle, there is a *net* export of one positive charge each turn — so the pump itself nudges the inside slightly negative (a few mV). Run it continuously against constant leak and the gradients reach a steady level: the charged battery the neuron lives on.

### Why it's true / how it works

The pump is **electrogenic** (net charge moved per cycle is nonzero), so it directly contributes a small voltage. But its main job is *maintaining the concentration gradients* — the reservoirs that the Nernst/Goldman machinery turns into the resting and action potentials. Restoring these gradients after activity is a neuron's single largest energy cost, consuming roughly half the brain's entire energy budget. Neural signaling is therefore fundamentally an energy-management problem.

### Where it connects

These gradients are the raw material for **nernst** (per-ion target voltage), **goldman** (the blended resting voltage), **resting-potential** (a steady state held by the pump), and every **action-potential** (a brief, controlled discharge of the battery). Myelination in **saltatory-conduction** is partly an *energy* trick: fewer ions enter, so less pumping is needed.

### Watch out

A frequent error is calling the resting state an "equilibrium." It is not. The pump runs nonstop, burning ATP, to hold the cell *away* from equilibrium. Stop the pump (or the oxygen that makes the ATP) and the gradients slowly run down, the battery discharges, and signaling fails — which is exactly why the brain is so vulnerable to even brief loss of blood flow.

atoms.title: Nernst equilibrium potential
atoms.summary: For a single permeant ion, the membrane voltage at which diffusion and electrical drift exactly cancel.

depths.eli5: Charged particles (ions) naturally drift from where they are crowded to where they are sparse — that's just spreading out. But because ions carry electric charge, a voltage across the cell's skin can push them the other way. The Nernst potential is the exact voltage at which those two pushes — spreading-out versus electrical-pull — perfectly cancel, so the ion stops moving on net. Think of it as the 'tie score' voltage for one kind of ion.
depths.core: Suppose the cell membrane let only one ion, call it X, pass through. The voltage would settle at a value labeled E_X (the equilibrium or Nernst potential for X), where the concentration gradient pushing X one way is exactly balanced by the electrical gradient pushing it back, so no net current flows. In the equation, R is the gas constant, T is temperature, F is the Faraday constant, z is the ion's charge, and the ratio is the concentration outside over inside. At body temperature the lumped factor RT/F is about 26.7 mV, so a 10-fold concentration difference gives roughly ±61 mV (sign depending on the charge). For real neurons, potassium gives E_K ≈ −90 mV and sodium gives E_Na ≈ +60 mV.
depths.deep: The Nernst potential is an equilibrium statement — the voltage of zero net current for that ion — obtained by setting the ion's electrochemical potential equal on both sides of the membrane. It is the per-ion 'target voltage' that the real membrane gets pulled toward, more strongly for ions the membrane lets through more easily (higher conductance). This is the foundation for the Goldman equation (which blends several ions) and for the standard mental model of each channel type as a tiny battery (its E_X) wired in series with a resistor (its conductance).

atoms.note: 61 mV per tenfold concentration change (per 'decade'), for a singly charged ion at 37 °C, is the number worth memorizing.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Charged particles (ions) naturally spread from where they are crowded to where they are sparse — that is just diffusion. But because ions carry charge, a voltage across the membrane can push them the other way. The **Nernst potential** is the exact voltage at which these two pushes — diffusion outward versus electrical pull inward — perfectly cancel, so the ion stops moving *on net*. Think of it as the "tie-score" voltage for one kind of ion.

### Precisely

If the membrane let only one ion $X$ through, the voltage would settle at its equilibrium (Nernst) potential

$$E_X = \frac{RT}{zF}\ln\frac{[X]_{out}}{[X]_{in}}$$

where $R$ is the gas constant, $T$ the absolute temperature (kelvin), $F$ the Faraday constant, $z$ the ion's charge, and the ratio is concentration outside over inside. At body temperature the lumped factor $RT/F \approx 26.7\,\text{mV}$.

### Worked example

Take a singly charged cation ($z=+1$) that is $10\times$ more concentrated outside than inside, at $37\,^\circ\text{C}$:

$$E_X = \frac{RT}{F}\ln 10 \approx 26.7\,\text{mV} \times 2.303 \approx +61\,\text{mV}.$$

The sign is positive because the cation "wants" to flow inward (down its gradient), so it takes a *positive* inside voltage to hold it back. Real neurons: potassium is high inside, giving $E_K \approx -90\,\text{mV}$; sodium is high outside, giving $E_{Na} \approx +60\,\text{mV}$. The number to memorize: **about $61\,\text{mV}$ per tenfold (per decade) concentration difference** for a monovalent ion at body temperature.

### Why it's true / how it works

Set the *electrochemical potential* of the ion equal on both sides of the membrane. The chemical part is $RT\ln[X]$; the electrical part is $zFV$. Demanding they balance and solving for $V$ gives the Nernst equation directly. It is an **equilibrium** statement — the voltage of *zero net current* for that one ion — not a description of how fast the ion moves.

### Where it connects

The Nernst potential is the per-ion "target voltage" that the membrane is pulled toward, more strongly for ions it passes more easily. It is the building block for the **goldman** equation (which blends several ions) and the **resting-potential**. It also licenses the standard mental model used in **hodgkin-huxley**: each channel type is a tiny battery ($E_X$) in series with a resistor (its conductance).

### Watch out

A common slip is forgetting the charge $z$ and the sign. For chloride ($\text{Cl}^-$, $z=-1$) the equation flips, so you can write it with the concentration ratio inverted. Also: $E_X$ tells you the *resting target* of one ion, not the cell's actual voltage — the real membrane is permeable to several ions at once, which is the job of Goldman.

### Worth knowing

Because the relationship is *logarithmic*, the membrane is far more sensitive to changes in the *low*-concentration side than the high side — which is exactly why small shifts in *extracellular* potassium (normally only $\sim 4\,\text{mM}$) can dangerously change $E_K$ and hence excitability, a real clinical concern in heart and nerve. The Nernst potential is also called the **reversal potential** because it is the voltage at which the current through a channel *reverses* direction (inward below it, outward above it) — a property experimentalists use to identify *which* ion a channel passes: find the voltage where its current is zero and compare to the known equilibrium potentials. This makes $E_X$ not just a theoretical balance point but a measurable fingerprint of channel selectivity.

atoms.title: Goldman–Hodgkin–Katz voltage equation
atoms.summary: The resting potential is a permeability-weighted blend of the individual ions' equilibrium potentials.

depths.eli5: A real cell membrane lets several kinds of ions through at once, not just one. So instead of a single tie-score voltage, the cell's actual voltage is a weighted average of all of them. The trick: an ion the membrane lets through easily gets a loud vote; an ion it barely lets through gets a quiet vote. Whichever ion passes most easily mostly decides the voltage.
depths.core: When several ions can cross, the membrane voltage V_m is not any single ion's Nernst potential but a weighted blend, where each ion is weighted by its permeability P (how easily that ion crosses the membrane). In the equation, [K]_o means potassium concentration outside, [K]_i inside, and so on for sodium (Na) and chloride (Cl). At rest the membrane lets potassium through far more easily than sodium, so V_m (about −70 mV) sits near E_K (−90 mV) but is nudged toward E_Na (+60 mV) by a small steady sodium leak. Chloride (Cl⁻) appears with its inside/outside concentrations flipped because it is negatively charged.
depths.deep: The Goldman–Hodgkin–Katz (GHK) equation is derived under the 'constant-field assumption' (the electric field across the thin membrane is treated as uniform) and assumes each ion's flow is independent of the others. Its real power is dynamic: an action potential is essentially a brief surge in P_Na (sodium permeability) that drags V_m from near E_K up toward E_Na and back down. David Goldman (1943) and later Alan Hodgkin with Bernard Katz (1949) used it to turn the resting voltage from a mystery into something you can predict from a simple ratio of permeabilities.

atoms.note: At rest the membrane is far more permeable to K⁺ than to Na⁺, so it 'votes' mostly for E_K; during a spike that permeability ratio briefly flips.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

A real membrane lets several ions through at once, not just one — so the cell's voltage cannot be any *single* ion's tie-score. Instead it is a *weighted average* of all the per-ion target voltages. The trick: an ion the membrane passes easily gets a loud vote; an ion it barely passes gets a quiet whisper. Whichever ion crosses most easily mostly decides the voltage.

### Precisely

When several ions can cross, the membrane voltage is the **Goldman–Hodgkin–Katz (GHK)** value

$$V_m = \frac{RT}{F}\ln\frac{P_{K}[K]_o + P_{Na}[Na]_o + P_{Cl}[Cl]_i}{P_{K}[K]_i + P_{Na}[Na]_i + P_{Cl}[Cl]_o}$$

where each $P$ is a **permeability** (how easily that ion crosses), subscripts $o$ and $i$ mean outside and inside, and chloride ($\text{Cl}^-$, being negative) appears with its concentrations flipped.

### Worked example

At rest a typical neuron has $P_K : P_{Na} \approx 1 : 0.04$ — potassium far more permeant. Plug in roughly $[K]_o=4$, $[K]_i=140$, $[Na]_o=145$, $[Na]_i=12$ (mM). Because $P_K$ dominates the sums, the logarithm sits close to $\ln([K]_o/[K]_i)$, pulling $V_m$ near $E_K\approx-90\,\text{mV}$ — but the small $P_{Na}$ term nudges it up to about $-70\,\text{mV}$. Now imagine the spike: $P_{Na}$ jumps to roughly $20\times P_K$. The numerator becomes sodium-dominated, the log flips sign, and $V_m$ races toward $E_{Na}\approx+60\,\text{mV}$.

### Why it's true / how it works

GHK is derived under the **constant-field assumption** (the electric field across the thin membrane is treated as uniform) and assumes each ion flows independently of the others. The headline insight is dynamic: an **action-potential** is essentially a brief surge in $P_{Na}$ that drags $V_m$ from near $E_K$ up toward $E_{Na}$ and back. Goldman (1943), then Hodgkin and Katz (1949), turned the resting voltage from a mystery into a predictable ratio of permeabilities.

### Where it connects

GHK blends many **nernst** potentials into one number; it explains the **resting-potential** and the depolarizing phase of the **action-potential**. The "permeability that changes with voltage and time" is exactly what **voltage-gated-channels** and the **hodgkin-huxley** model make precise.

### Watch out

Permeability is *not* concentration. Raising an ion's permeability moves $V_m$ toward *that ion's* Nernst potential; raising its concentration changes the Nernst potential itself. Confusing the two is the classic GHK error. Also note GHK assumes independent ion flow — it breaks down for channels where ions queue single-file.

### Worth knowing

A useful sanity check: if you set every permeability except one to zero, GHK collapses exactly back to the **nernst** equation for that single ion — confirming Nernst is the special case and Goldman the general blend. The permeabilities themselves are *ratios* (only their relative sizes matter), which is why experimentalists report things like $P_{Na}/P_K$ rather than absolute values. Finally, GHK is a *steady-state* voltage formula, not a dynamical equation: it tells you where $V_m$ will settle for a *fixed* set of permeabilities, but during a real spike the permeabilities change far faster than $V_m$ can equilibrate, which is why the full **hodgkin-huxley** differential equations — not GHK alone — are needed to trace the action potential moment by moment.

atoms.title: The resting membrane potential
atoms.summary: At rest a neuron sits near −70 mV, a dynamic steady state held by leak permeabilities and the pump, not a true equilibrium.

depths.eli5: Even when a neuron is doing nothing, the inside of the cell holds a steady voltage of about −70 millivolts (negative, meaning the inside is more negatively charged than the outside). 'Resting' doesn't mean frozen: ions are constantly leaking across the membrane, and a pump keeps working in the background to refill the battery and hold that voltage steady. The neuron pays energy just to stay idle.
depths.core: The resting membrane potential is the steady voltage at which the total electric current flowing across the membrane is zero (everything balances). Because the resting membrane is most permeable to potassium, V_m sits close to E_K (about −90 mV) but is dragged up to roughly −70 mV by a constant small sodium leak — exactly what the Goldman equation predicts. The Na⁺/K⁺ pump runs nonstop to replace the ions that leak through, so 'rest' is an actively maintained state, not a passive one.

The cell pays energy continuously just to stay still. This standing potential is the operating point from which depolarizations are measured and the baseline the action potential springs from.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Even when a neuron is doing nothing, the inside holds a steady voltage of about $-70$ millivolts — meaning the interior is more negatively charged than the outside. "Resting" does not mean frozen. Ions are constantly leaking across the membrane, and the pump works in the background to refill the battery and hold the voltage steady. The neuron pays energy just to stay idle.

### Precisely

The **resting membrane potential** is the steady voltage at which the *total* electric current across the membrane is zero — every inward leak is balanced by an outward one. Because the resting membrane is most permeable to potassium, $V_m$ sits close to $E_K\approx-90\,\text{mV}$ but is dragged up to roughly $-70\,\text{mV}$ by a constant small sodium leak — exactly what the **goldman** equation predicts. The $\text{Na}^+/\text{K}^+$ pump runs nonstop to replace the leaked ions.

### Worked example

Track the currents at $-70\,\text{mV}$. Potassium is above its equilibrium ($E_K=-90$), so $K^+$ leaks *out*, carrying positive charge out (an outward current). Sodium is far below its equilibrium ($E_{Na}=+60$), so $Na^+$ leaks *in* (an inward current). At exactly $-70\,\text{mV}$ these leak currents (plus the pump's small contribution) sum to zero, so the voltage holds. Block the pump and the gradients slowly collapse; the cell depolarizes toward $0\,\text{mV}$ and signaling dies.

### Why it's true / how it works

Crucially this is a **steady state**, not thermodynamic equilibrium. Each ion is *off* its own Nernst potential, so each one continuously leaks down its gradient; the pump spends ATP to keep the gradients constant. Zero *net* current does not mean zero *individual* current — it means the individual currents cancel while the pump quietly restores what leaked. The cell is held away from equilibrium, burning fuel to stand still.

### Where it connects

The resting potential is the operating point from which every signal is measured: a **depolarization** is a rise from here, the **action-potential** springs from here once threshold is crossed, and **synaptic-integration** sums EPSPs and IPSPs relative to this baseline. It follows directly from **ionic-gradients** (the batteries) and **goldman** (the blend).

### Watch out

The biggest misconception is "equilibrium." A true equilibrium needs no energy input; the resting potential needs the pump running forever. A second trap: the resting value is not a universal constant — different neurons (and glia, and muscle) sit at different resting voltages because they have different channel mixes and therefore different permeability ratios.

### Worth knowing

A common confusion is *how many ions actually move*. Strikingly few: the resting potential is set by a thin layer of charge right at the membrane, so only a tiny fraction of the cell's ions need to redistribute to establish $-70\,\text{mV}$ — the bulk concentrations barely change on the timescale of a single spike. This is why a neuron can fire many times before the pump's slow restoration becomes limiting. It also explains why blocking the pump does not instantly abolish the resting potential: the gradients (the real batteries) persist for a while and only run down gradually. Different cell types tune their resting value by expressing different "leak" potassium channels, which is how, for example, some neurons rest closer to threshold and are intrinsically more excitable than others.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Think of a nerve fiber as a leaky garden hose. Inject a little voltage at one spot and it does *not* travel far cleanly — it spreads out, weakens, and smears over distance and time, because the "hose" leaks current through its walls. "Passive" means we are looking at small, below-threshold signals — too weak to trigger a spike. On their own, they just fade.

### Precisely

Below threshold a stretch of membrane behaves like a **resistor–capacitor (RC)** cable, governed by the **cable equation**

$$\tau_m\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} = \lambda^2\frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial x^2} - V.$$

Two constants summarize it. The **membrane time constant** $\tau_m = R_m C_m$ (resistance $\times$ capacitance) sets how *sluggish* the voltage is in time. The **length constant** $\lambda = \sqrt{R_m/R_i}$ ($R_i$ = internal axial resistance) sets how *far* a steady voltage spreads before shrinking to $1/e\approx 37\%$ of its starting size.

### Worked example

Inject a steady current into a dendrite with $\lambda = 0.5\,\text{mm}$. At the injection site the voltage is, say, $10\,\text{mV}$. One length constant away ($0.5\,\text{mm}$) it has fallen to $10\times e^{-1}\approx 3.7\,\text{mV}$; two length constants away ($1.0\,\text{mm}$) it is $10\times e^{-2}\approx 1.35\,\text{mV}$. So a synapse far out on a thin dendrite delivers a much smaller bump at the soma than one nearby — the cell's *shape* discounts distant inputs.

### Why it's true / how it works

The cable equation is a *diffusion equation with a leak term*: charge injected at a point both spreads along the inside (set by $R_i$) and leaks out across the membrane (set by $R_m$, $C_m$). Their competition gives the exponential spatial decay over $\lambda$ and the exponential temporal rise/fall over $\tau_m$. Thick, well-insulated fibers have large $\lambda$ and so carry passive signals farther — which is exactly why myelin helps.

### Where it connects

$\tau_m$ and $\lambda$ are the "pixel size" of a neuron's integration in time and space — the raw substrate of **synaptic-integration** (temporal summation lives within $\tau_m$; spatial summation is shaped by $\lambda$). Because passive spread dies within millimeters, an actively regenerating **action-potential** is *necessary* for long-distance signaling, and **saltatory-conduction** exploits a large $\lambda$ to jump between nodes.

### Watch out

Don't confuse $\tau_m$ (time) with $\lambda$ (space) — they answer different questions ("how slow?" vs "how far?"). And remember the cable model is strictly *subthreshold*: once voltage-gated channels open, the membrane stops being passive and the linear cable equation no longer applies.

### Worth knowing

Rall's great insight was that a complicated branching dendrite can often be collapsed into an *equivalent cylinder* under certain diameter rules, making the math tractable and revealing how branch geometry sets integration. Two practical consequences follow from the cable equation. First, because signals slow and smear as they travel, a neuron has an effective *integration time window* — inputs separated by much more than $\tau_m$ cannot sum. Second, the same physics that limits passive spread is what lets dendrites *compartmentalize*: a distal branch can run a local computation (even a local spike) that the soma only partly "sees," so one neuron hosts several semi-independent processing zones. These ideas turn the cable equation from a decay formula into a theory of dendritic computation.

atoms.title: Voltage-gated ion channels
atoms.summary: Membrane proteins whose pores open and close in response to voltage, providing the nonlinearity that makes spikes possible.

depths.eli5: These are tiny doors built into the cell's outer skin, made of protein. Each door can feel the voltage across the membrane and opens or shuts in response. When the voltage rises past a tipping point, sodium doors fly open, sodium rushes in, and that raises the voltage even more — which opens still more doors. This self-feeding chain reaction is exactly what makes a nerve signal explode into a full spike.
depths.core: A 'voltage-gated ion channel' is a protein pore that opens or closes depending on the membrane voltage. The sodium (Na⁺) and potassium (K⁺) versions each contain a charged part called the voltage sensor (built from protein segments known as S4 helices) that physically moves when the membrane depolarizes (its voltage becomes less negative), pulling the pore open. The key is timing: sodium channels open fast and then 'inactivate' (auto-shut even though the voltage is still high), while potassium channels open more slowly and stay open. Fast sodium = quick positive feedback that drives the spike up; delayed potassium plus sodium shut-off = negative feedback that brings it back down. That timing difference is the engine of the action potential.
depths.deep: Each channel is selective — it lets the right ion through and blocks others — thanks to a narrow 'selectivity filter' lined with specific atoms (the potassium channel's filter, encoded by a signature stretch of protein, grips potassium ions after stripping off their water coat). 'Gating' is how the moving voltage sensor opens and closes the pore. Sodium-channel inactivation works by a separate 'ball-and-chain' plug that swings in to block the pore; this limits how long each spike lasts and creates a refractory period (a brief recovery time after a spike during which the cell can't easily fire again). That refractory period caps the maximum firing rate and gives spikes their all-or-none, one-direction-only character.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

These are tiny doors built into the membrane, made of protein. Each door can *feel* the voltage across the membrane and opens or shuts in response. When the voltage rises past a tipping point, **sodium doors** fly open, sodium rushes in, and that raises the voltage even more — which opens still more doors. This self-feeding chain reaction is exactly what makes a nerve signal explode into a full spike.

### Precisely

A **voltage-gated ion channel** is a protein pore whose opening depends on membrane voltage. The sodium ($\text{Na}^+$) and potassium ($\text{K}^+$) versions each contain a charged **voltage sensor** (built from protein segments called S4 helices) that physically moves when the membrane **depolarizes** (becomes less negative), pulling the pore open. The decisive feature is *timing*: $\text{Na}^+$ channels open **fast** and then **inactivate** (auto-shut even while the voltage stays high), while $\text{K}^+$ channels open **slowly** and stay open.

### Worked example

Hold a patch of membrane at rest and then step it to $-40\,\text{mV}$. Within a fraction of a millisecond the $\text{Na}^+$ sensors move and the channels open — inward sodium current surges, depolarizing the patch further and opening yet more $\text{Na}^+$ channels (positive feedback). A millisecond or so later two things happen together: the $\text{Na}^+$ channels' inactivation gates swing shut, *and* the slow $\text{K}^+$ channels finally open and let potassium out. Together these end the surge and drive the voltage back down. That fast-up / delayed-down sequence is one spike.

### Why it's true / how it works

Each channel is **selective**, passing the right ion via a narrow **selectivity filter** (the $\text{K}^+$ filter grips potassium after stripping its water coat). **Gating** is the sensor-driven opening/closing of the pore. $\text{Na}^+$ **inactivation** uses a separate "ball-and-chain" plug that swings in to block the pore; this caps how long each spike lasts and creates the **refractory period** — a brief recovery time during which the cell cannot easily fire again. That refractory period limits maximum firing rate and gives spikes their one-way, all-or-none character.

### Where it connects

Fast $\text{Na}^+$ opening (positive feedback) plus delayed $\text{K}^+$ opening and $\text{Na}^+$ auto-shutdown (negative feedback) *is* the **action-potential**. The **hodgkin-huxley** model captures these kinetics quantitatively with its $m$, $h$, $n$ gating variables. Clustered $\text{Na}^+$ channels at nodes drive **saltatory-conduction**, and voltage-gated $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ channels are the trigger in the **chemical-synapse**.

### Watch out

"Inactivated" is not the same as "closed." A closed channel can reopen immediately; an *inactivated* one is blocked and must first recover (the membrane usually has to repolarize) before it can open again. Forgetting this distinction makes the refractory period — and the spike's one-way travel — impossible to explain.

### Worth knowing

It is worth distinguishing the three states a voltage-gated channel cycles through: **closed** (resting, ready to open), **open** (conducting), and **inactivated** (blocked, *not* ready to reopen). The transition open$\to$inactivated$\to$closed must run in order, and the cell usually has to repolarize before inactivated channels reset to closed — which is the molecular root of the refractory period and of one-way spike travel. These channels are also the targets of a remarkable pharmacology: local anesthetics and several natural toxins (tetrodotoxin from pufferfish, for instance) plug the sodium channel and abolish spikes, while many inherited "channelopathies" — certain epilepsies, cardiac arrhythmias, and pain syndromes — trace to single mutations that shift a channel's voltage-dependence or its inactivation kinetics by just a few millivolts. That such tiny biophysical changes cause whole-body disease underscores how finely the spike depends on precise channel timing.

atoms.title: The action potential
atoms.summary: An all-or-none, self-regenerating voltage spike that carries digital signals down the axon without loss.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

The action potential is the actual nerve signal — a quick, sharp pulse of voltage. The sequence: when the voltage at the trigger zone climbs past a tipping point (the **threshold**), a chain reaction lets sodium flood in, so the voltage shoots up steeply, then snaps back down. That pulse then travels along the axon like a row of dominoes falling, each patch knocking over the next, so the signal arrives at the far end *at full strength* instead of fading.

### Precisely

When the membrane depolarizes past **threshold**, voltage-gated $\text{Na}^+$ channels open; inflowing sodium pushes the voltage higher, opening still more channels — runaway positive feedback that drives $V_m$ toward $E_{Na}\approx+60\,\text{mV}$. Then $\text{Na}^+$ channels **inactivate** and slower $\text{K}^+$ channels let potassium out, **repolarizing** the membrane, often dipping briefly below rest (the **after-hyperpolarization**). The spike is **all-or-none**: its amplitude carries no information — only *whether* and *when* it fires.

### Worked example

A neuron sits at $-70\,\text{mV}$. Summed synaptic input nudges the trigger zone to $-55\,\text{mV}$ (threshold). Sodium channels open en masse; within about $1\,\text{ms}$ the voltage rockets up to roughly $+40\,\text{mV}$ (the peak). Sodium inactivates, potassium flows out, and over the next millisecond or two the voltage falls back through rest to about $-80\,\text{mV}$ before settling. Crucially, doubling the original stimulus does *not* make a bigger spike — it just makes spikes come *sooner* or *more often*.

### Why it's true / how it works

Because the spike **regenerates** at every membrane patch (each depolarized patch brings the next patch to threshold), it travels the whole axon without shrinking — solving the decay problem that limits passive **passive-cable** spread. The **refractory period** (set by $\text{Na}^+$ inactivation) makes the signal travel one way only, since the patch just behind is temporarily unexcitable. In effect, the action potential is the neuron's analog-to-digital converter: graded dendritic input goes in; a clean digital train of spike *times* comes out.

### Where it connects

The spike is the output of **voltage-gated-channels**, modeled exactly by **hodgkin-huxley**, sped up by **saltatory-conduction**, and abstracted to its essentials by **integrate-and-fire**. Its all-or-none nature is *why* information lives in **neural-coding** (rate and timing), not amplitude.

### Watch out

"All-or-none" trips people up: a stronger stimulus does **not** make a taller spike. It changes spike *timing* and *frequency*. Also, threshold is not a fixed voltage carved in stone — it depends on how many $\text{Na}^+$ channels are available, which is why a cell is harder to fire right after a spike (the refractory period).

### Worth knowing

The refractory period comes in two flavors worth distinguishing: an **absolute** refractory period (no stimulus, however strong, can fire a second spike, because the sodium channels are inactivated) followed by a **relative** refractory period (a stronger-than-normal stimulus *can* fire, as channels recover and the after-hyperpolarization fades). Together these set a ceiling on firing rate — typically a few hundred hertz at most. Spikes also normally start at the **axon initial segment** and then propagate *both* down the axon (orthodromic) and backward into the dendrites (the back-propagating spike that **stdp** exploits as a "you fired" signal). And because conduction is just the spike repeatedly re-igniting the next patch, anything that lowers channel availability — local anesthetics, certain toxins — blocks propagation by breaking that chain.

atoms.title: The Hodgkin–Huxley model
atoms.summary: A quantitative conductance-based model that reconstructs the action potential from voltage- and time-dependent gating variables.

depths.eli5: Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley wrote down a set of equations describing how the tiny voltage-sensing doors in a nerve membrane open and close over time. When you let those equations run, they reproduce a real nerve spike almost perfectly. This was a landmark: the first time a living signal in the brain was fully predicted, in detail, by mathematics.
depths.core: Hodgkin and Huxley (1952) used the 'voltage clamp' — a technique that holds a cell at a fixed voltage so you can measure the current flowing — on the giant axon of a squid (large enough to insert electrodes). They modeled the membrane as a capacitor (charge store) wired in parallel with three conductances: one for sodium, one for potassium, and a constant 'leak.' Each conductance rises and falls according to gating variables — m and h control the sodium conductance, n controls the potassium conductance — and each variable obeys a simple rate law whose speed depends on voltage. Numerically solving the four linked equations on a computer reproduces the real spike's shape, its threshold, its refractoriness (recovery time), and how fast it travels.
depths.deep: The exponents in the equation (m³h for sodium, n⁴ for potassium) encode the idea that several independent gating 'particles' must all be in the open position at once for the channel to conduct — a strikingly accurate guess about the channels' multi-part structure, made decades before anyone could read a channel's genetic sequence. This model is the founding artifact of computational neuroscience: it proved a biological process could be captured exactly as a system of differential equations (equations describing rates of change). It earned the 1963 Nobel Prize and seeded every 'conductance-based' neuron simulator since.

atoms.note: The m³h and n⁴ exponents were inspired guesses about multiple gating particles — later vindicated by the four-domain / four-subunit architecture of the actual channels.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley wrote down a set of equations describing how the voltage-sensing doors in a nerve membrane open and close over time. Let those equations run on a computer and they reproduce a real nerve spike almost perfectly — its shape, its threshold, its recovery. It was the first time a living signal in the brain was fully *predicted*, in quantitative detail, by mathematics.

### Precisely

Modeling the membrane as a capacitor in parallel with three conductances (sodium, potassium, leak), the current balance is

$$C_m\frac{dV}{dt} = -g_{Na}m^3h\,(V-E_{Na}) - g_{K}n^4\,(V-E_K) - g_L(V-E_L) + I.$$

Here $C_m$ is membrane capacitance; $g_{Na}, g_K, g_L$ are maximal conductances; $E_{Na}, E_K, E_L$ are the **nernst** potentials; $I$ is injected current. The **gating variables** $m$ (Na activation), $h$ (Na inactivation), and $n$ (K activation) each range $0$–$1$ and obey first-order kinetics whose rates depend on voltage.

### Worked example

Inject a brief current $I$. The $-g_L(V-E_L)$ leak term resists it, but if $V$ rises enough, the voltage-dependent rates make $m$ climb fast toward $1$ — and because the Na term scales as $m^3$, the sodium conductance rises *steeply*, pouring in inward current and driving $V$ up further. A beat later $h$ falls (sodium inactivates) and $n$ rises (potassium activates, scaling as $n^4$), so the outward potassium current dominates and $V$ collapses back. Numerically stepping these four coupled equations traces out a textbook action potential.

### Why it's true / how it works

Hodgkin and Huxley used the **voltage clamp** — a feedback circuit that holds the cell at a chosen voltage so the membrane current can be measured directly — on the **squid giant axon**, large enough to insert electrodes. The exponents $m^3h$ and $n^4$ encode the idea that several independent gating "particles" must *all* be open at once for the channel to conduct — a strikingly accurate guess about multi-part channel structure, made decades before channel genes could be read.

### Where it connects

This is the quantitative engine behind the **action-potential** and the kinetics of **voltage-gated-channels**. It is the founding artifact of computational neuroscience and the parent of every conductance-based simulator; **integrate-and-fire** is its deliberate simplification, and **neuronal-dynamics** analyzes its bifurcation structure.

### Watch out

The gating variables are *probabilities/fractions*, not currents — don't read $m$ as "sodium current." And the famous exponents were an *empirical fit*, not a derivation; their later vindication by the four-domain Na channel and four-subunit K channel is a happy confirmation, not something the model proved on its own.

### Worth knowing

A subtle point that vindicates the whole approach: Hodgkin and Huxley measured each conductance's voltage-dependence *separately* (using ion substitution and the voltage clamp to isolate the sodium and potassium currents), fit simple rate equations to those isolated measurements, and *then* let the assembled model run in *current* mode — and it predicted the free-running action potential they had never fit it to. That out-of-sample prediction is what elevated the work from curve-fitting to genuine mechanistic theory. The model also correctly predicted the *threshold*, the *refractory period*, and the *conduction velocity* of the propagating spike, all as emergent consequences of the gating kinetics rather than as separately tuned parameters.

atoms.title: Myelin & saltatory conduction
atoms.summary: Insulating myelin forces the spike to jump between nodes of Ranvier, vastly speeding conduction at low metabolic cost.

depths.eli5: Many axons are wrapped in a fatty insulating sleeve called myelin, with small bare gaps left along the way. Instead of crawling slowly along every inch of the fiber, the signal leaps from bare gap to bare gap — much faster, like a stone skipping across water instead of rolling along the bottom. 'Saltatory' just means 'jumping.'
depths.core: Helper cells called glia (oligodendrocytes in the brain and spinal cord, Schwann cells in the body's peripheral nerves) wrap the axon in myelin. The myelin makes those wrapped stretches leak less current (higher resistance) and store less charge (lower capacitance). The voltage-gated sodium channels that regenerate the spike are bunched up only at the bare gaps — the nodes of Ranvier — between myelin segments. So the spike fires fresh at each node, then spreads quickly and passively along the insulated stretch (the internode) to the next node, appearing to jump, or 'saltate,' from node to node.
depths.deep: Myelin increases the length constant λ (how far passive voltage spreads) and lowers the membrane capacitance C_m, so the passive jump between nodes is both longer and faster, while active regeneration at the nodes keeps the signal from decaying. The payoff is conduction speeds up to about 120 meters per second in large myelinated fibers, versus roughly 1 m/s in bare ones — and far fewer sodium ions enter, so much less energy is spent pumping them back out. It is a joint win on both speed and energy. When myelin is damaged — as in multiple sclerosis, a disease that strips it — conduction slows or fails.

quiz.answer: Speed: larger λ and lower capacitance let passive spread between nodes be fast, raising conduction velocity. Energy: regenerating only at nodes means far fewer Na⁺ ions enter, so less ATP is needed to restore gradients.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Many axons are wrapped in a fatty insulating sleeve called **myelin**, with small bare gaps left along the way. Instead of crawling slowly along every inch of the fiber, the signal *leaps* from bare gap to bare gap — far faster, like a stone skipping across water instead of rolling along the bottom. "Saltatory" simply means "jumping."

### Precisely

Helper cells called **glia** — oligodendrocytes in the brain and spinal cord, Schwann cells in peripheral nerves — wrap the axon in myelin. Myelinated stretches **leak less current** (higher $R_m$) and **store less charge** (lower $C_m$). The voltage-gated $\text{Na}^+$ channels that regenerate the spike are clustered only at the bare gaps, the **nodes of Ranvier**. So the spike fires fresh at one node, spreads quickly and passively along the insulated **internode**, and re-fires at the next node — appearing to jump.

### Worked example

Compare two axons. A bare $1\,\mu\text{m}$ fiber conducts at roughly $1\,\text{m/s}$, regenerating at every micron — slow and ion-hungry. A myelinated fiber with nodes spaced $\sim 1\,\text{mm}$ apart only fires at the nodes; between them the spike spreads passively along a high-$\lambda$, low-$C_m$ internode, so conduction can reach about $120\,\text{m/s}$. Because sodium enters *only at the nodes*, far fewer ions cross per spike, so the pump has far less to clean up afterward.

### Why it's true / how it works

Recall the **passive-cable**: myelin *raises* the length constant $\lambda = \sqrt{R_m/R_i}$ (more insulation $\to$ larger $R_m$) and *lowers* the capacitance $C_m$ (less charge to fill). A larger $\lambda$ lets the passive jump reach the next node before decaying; a lower $C_m$ makes that jump fast. Active regeneration at each node keeps the signal from ever dying. It is a joint win on **speed and energy**.

### Where it connects

This atom combines **action-potential** (the regenerated spike) with **passive-cable** (the fast internodal spread). The energy savings tie back to **ionic-gradients** (less pumping). When myelin is stripped — as in **multiple sclerosis** — conduction slows or fails, a direct clinical consequence of these physics.

### Watch out

A subtle misconception: the spike does *not* literally teleport across a dark internode. It still travels there — but *passively and fast*, not by regenerating. And node spacing matters: too far apart and the passive signal would decay below threshold before reaching the next node, so myelin geometry is finely tuned, not arbitrary.

### Worth knowing

Conduction velocity in myelinated fibers scales roughly *linearly* with axon diameter, whereas in bare fibers it scales only with the *square root* of diameter — so myelin buys speed far more cheaply (in space and metabolic cost) than simply growing fatter axons would. This is why vertebrates could pack fast, long-range wiring into a compact nervous system. Myelination is also not fixed at birth: it continues into adulthood and can be tuned by experience ("activity-dependent myelination"), subtly adjusting conduction delays — which matters because precise *timing* between distant regions depends on these delays. Finally, the *clustering* of sodium channels at nodes depends on signals from the myelinating glia, so demyelination not only removes insulation but eventually disperses the channels, compounding the conduction failure.

atoms.title: The chemical synapse
atoms.summary: At most synapses, a presynaptic spike triggers Ca²⁺-dependent neurotransmitter release that changes the postsynaptic cell's voltage.

depths.eli5: Where two neurons meet there's a tiny gap called a synapse. When a spike arrives at the end of the first neuron, it can't jump the gap electrically, so instead it squirts out chemical messengers. Those chemicals drift across the gap and land on the second neuron, nudging it either toward firing or away from firing. This is how most neurons talk to each other.
depths.core: When the spike reaches the axon terminal, it opens voltage-gated calcium (Ca²⁺) channels. Calcium rushing in triggers little membrane sacs called vesicles — each pre-filled with neurotransmitter (the chemical messenger) — to fuse with the cell's edge and dump their contents into the gap (a process called exocytosis). The transmitter drifts across the synaptic cleft (about 20 nanometers wide) and binds receptors on the receiving (postsynaptic) cell, opening ion channels there. This produces a small, graded postsynaptic potential — either excitatory (an EPSP, nudging toward firing) or inhibitory (an IPSP, nudging away). Transmission goes one way only and takes a short delay of about 0.5–1 millisecond.
depths.deep: Release is 'quantal': vesicles deliver fixed-size packets, so the receiving cell's response comes in whole-number multiples of one vesicle's effect (Bernard Katz's quantal hypothesis). Calcium is the trigger because the molecular fusion machinery (the SNARE proteins plus a calcium sensor called synaptotagmin) is built to detect calcium — which makes release rise very steeply (roughly with the fourth power) as calcium concentration climbs. So a chemical synapse is not a plain wire: it is a chemically controlled relay that can be strengthened or weakened (it is 'plastic') and can flip sign between excite and inhibit — making it the basic unit of both computation and learning.

atoms.note: Quantal release (Katz): the receiving cell's responses come in whole-number multiples of a single-vesicle 'quantum.'

quiz.prompt: What does it mean that synaptic transmission is 'quantal'?
quiz.answer: Neurotransmitter is released in discrete packets (vesicles), so the postsynaptic response is an integer multiple of the response to a single vesicle's 'quantum'.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Where two neurons meet there is a tiny gap — a **synapse**. When a spike arrives at the end of the first neuron, it cannot jump the gap electrically, so instead it squirts out chemical messengers. Those chemicals drift across the gap and land on the second neuron, nudging it either toward firing or away from firing. This is how most neurons talk to each other.

### Precisely

When the spike reaches the axon terminal, it opens voltage-gated **calcium** ($\text{Ca}^{2+}$) channels. Inflowing calcium triggers membrane sacs called **vesicles** — each pre-filled with **neurotransmitter** — to fuse with the terminal membrane and dump their contents into the gap (**exocytosis**). The transmitter crosses the $\sim 20\,\text{nm}$ **synaptic cleft** and binds **receptors** on the **postsynaptic** cell, opening ion channels there. The result is a small **postsynaptic potential** — excitatory (**EPSP**, toward firing) or inhibitory (**IPSP**, away from firing) — after a delay of about $0.5$–$1\,\text{ms}$.

### Worked example

A spike invades the terminal and depolarizes it; $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ channels open and local calcium spikes from $\sim 100\,\text{nM}$ to tens of micromolar near the release sites. The calcium sensor **synaptotagmin**, working with the **SNARE** fusion proteins, detects this and triggers a few vesicles to fuse. Each vesicle releases a fixed packet of, say, glutamate, opening postsynaptic channels and producing an EPSP of a fraction of a millivolt. Because vesicles deliver fixed packets, the postsynaptic response comes in whole-number multiples of one vesicle's effect — Katz's **quantal** release.

### Why it's true / how it works

Calcium is the trigger because the fusion machinery is built to *detect* calcium, and release rises steeply (roughly with the *fourth power* of $[\text{Ca}^{2+}]$) — a tiny calcium change produces a large change in release. This steep, calcium-gated, one-way relay is what makes a chemical synapse far more than a wire: it can be strengthened or weakened (**plastic**) and can flip sign between excite and inhibit.

### Where it connects

The chemical synapse is the unit of **neurotransmitters-receptors** (which set sign and speed), the input to **synaptic-integration**, and the site of **ltp-ltd** and therefore **hebbian-learning**. Contrast it with the direct coupling of the **electrical-synapse**.

### Watch out

Don't assume the transmitter decides excitation or inhibition — the *receptor* does (the next atom). And "quantal" does not mean "one molecule": a quantum is one *vesicle's worth* of thousands of molecules, the smallest unit the synapse can release at once.

### Worth knowing

Beyond fixed-quantum release, synapses show fast **short-term plasticity**: with rapid repeated firing, some synapses *facilitate* (each successive pulse releases more, because residual calcium builds up) while others *depress* (the readily releasable vesicle pool runs down). This gives synapses a built-in, millisecond-scale memory that makes them act as temporal filters — facilitating synapses emphasize bursts, depressing synapses emphasize the *onset* of activity. The probability that any given vesicle releases on a spike (release probability) varies widely between synapses and is itself a tunable parameter, so two synapses with identical anatomy can transmit very differently. All of this sits *on top of* the slow LTP/LTD changes, giving the synapse a layered set of dynamics across timescales.

atoms.title: Electrical synapses & gap junctions
atoms.summary: Gap junctions directly couple neurons electrically, giving fast, bidirectional, near-instant signal transfer.

depths.eli5: Not all neurons use chemical messengers. Some are joined by direct microscopic tunnels, so electric current flows straight from the inside of one cell into the next with no gap to cross. That makes the connection extremely fast — there's no chemistry to wait for.
depths.core: At an electrical synapse, matching half-channels (called connexons, built from proteins called connexins) on two neighboring cells line up and dock to form a gap junction: a continuous pore that lets ions and small molecules pass directly between the two cells' interiors (their cytoplasms). Current flows with essentially no delay and usually in both directions, so connected neurons change voltage almost in lockstep. That makes electrical synapses ideal for synchronizing whole groups of neurons and for fast escape reflexes where every fraction of a millisecond counts.
depths.deep: Compared with chemical synapses, electrical synapses trade flexibility for raw speed. They have no transmission delay, no easy way to invert the sign (so they can't readily inhibit), and limited ability to strengthen or weaken — but they excel at keeping cells in sync. Real networks often mix both kinds: gap junctions linking inhibitory interneurons help generate coordinated gamma-band brain rhythms, while chemical synapses do most of the heavy computational work.

quiz.prompt: Name two functional differences between electrical and chemical synapses.
quiz.answer: Electrical synapses have essentially no synaptic delay and are usually bidirectional; chemical synapses have a ~0.5–1 ms delay, are unidirectional, can be excitatory or inhibitory, and are highly plastic.

quiz.prompt: Why are electrical synapses well suited to generating synchronized network oscillations?
quiz.answer: Their fast, bidirectional coupling makes connected neurons depolarize nearly simultaneously, promoting coherent population rhythms.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Not all neurons use chemical messengers. Some are joined by direct microscopic tunnels, so electric current flows straight from the inside of one cell into the next, with no gap to cross. That makes the connection extremely fast — there is no chemistry to wait for.

### Precisely

At an **electrical synapse**, matching half-channels called **connexons** (each built from six **connexin** proteins) on two neighboring cells line up and dock to form a **gap junction**: a continuous pore that lets ions and small molecules pass directly between the two cells' interiors (their **cytoplasms**). Current flows with essentially no delay and usually in *both* directions, so coupled neurons change voltage almost in lockstep.

### Worked example

Inject a depolarizing current into cell A. At a chemical synapse you would wait $\sim 0.5$–$1\,\text{ms}$ for vesicle release. At an electrical synapse, some of that current flows *immediately* through the gap-junction pores into cell B, so B's voltage rises within microseconds, tracking A. Reverse the injection (drive B instead) and current flows back into A — the coupling is bidirectional. This is ideal for fast escape reflexes and for keeping a group of cells synchronized.

### Why it's true / how it works

A gap junction is, electrically, a low-resistance resistor directly bridging two cells' interiors. Because no transmitter is released and no receptor must be activated, there is no synaptic delay and no easy way to invert the sign (so electrical synapses cannot readily *inhibit*). They also can't be strengthened or weakened as flexibly as chemical synapses. The trade is **flexibility for raw speed and synchrony**.

### Where it connects

Electrical synapses among inhibitory interneurons help generate the coordinated rhythms of **neural-oscillations** (especially gamma) and support the synchronized motifs in **neural-circuits**. They are the key exception to the strict discreteness of the **neuron-doctrine**, and a useful contrast to the chemically controlled **chemical-synapse**.

### Watch out

"Electrical" does not mean "more primitive" or "rare" — gap junctions are common in inhibitory networks and are essential for synchrony. But because they pass current in both directions and cannot easily invert sign, they are poor at the flexible, sign-switching computation that chemical synapses excel at. Real circuits usually *mix* both types.

### Worth knowing

Gap junctions are also **rectifying** in some cases — passing current more easily in one direction than the other — and their conductance can be *modulated* (for example, by intracellular pH, calcium, or phosphorylation), so even "fast and fixed" electrical synapses have a slow regulatory dial. Because the coupling is resistive, a gap junction acts as a **low-pass filter**: slow voltage changes pass between cells well, but fast spikes are partly attenuated, so coupled cells share their slow subthreshold fluctuations more faithfully than their individual spikes. This is precisely why electrical coupling among interneurons synchronizes *subthreshold* membrane potentials and helps pace network rhythms without forcing every cell to fire identical spikes. Developmentally, gap junctions are widespread in the immature brain and then prune back as chemical synapses mature — an early scaffolding role that later gives way to the more flexible chemical machinery.

atoms.title: Neurotransmitters & receptor types
atoms.summary: Transmitters act through fast ionotropic (channel) receptors and slow metabotropic (G-protein) receptors, setting a synapse's speed and sign.

depths.eli5: Neurotransmitters are the chemical messages neurons send. The receiving cell has 'locks' (receptors) that only certain messengers fit. Some locks, when opened, instantly swing a door open and let charged particles flood in. Other locks instead kick off a slower chain of events inside the cell. So the same gap can carry fast or slow signals depending on which lock the message lands on.
depths.core: Common neurotransmitters include glutamate (the main 'go' / excitatory signal), GABA and glycine (the main 'stop' / inhibitory signals), and modulators such as acetylcholine, dopamine, serotonin, and norepinephrine that adjust overall tone. Receptors come in two families. Ionotropic receptors (examples: AMPA, NMDA, GABA_A) are 'ligand-gated' channels — the messenger ('ligand') binds and the channel itself pops open, giving a response within milliseconds. Metabotropic receptors (examples: mGluR, and most dopamine and serotonin receptors) don't open a channel directly; they activate internal relay proteins (G proteins) and 'second messengers' inside the cell, producing slower effects lasting hundreds of milliseconds to minutes.
depths.deep: A crucial point: the synapse's sign (excite vs inhibit) is set by the receptor on the receiving cell, not by the transmitter alone. Glutamate opens channels that let in positive ions (excitatory); GABA acting on GABA_A receptors opens chloride channels (usually inhibitory). The NMDA receptor is special — it is gated by both the chemical AND the voltage (a magnesium ion, Mg²⁺, plugs it until the cell is depolarized). That makes it a molecular 'coincidence detector' that fires only when input and activity happen together — the linchpin of Hebbian learning (covered later). The slow, metabotropic pathway is the basis of neuromodulation, which retunes whole circuits at once.

atoms.note: The receptor, not the transmitter, sets a synapse's sign and speed — the same molecule can excite at one receptor and inhibit at another.

quiz.prompt: What is the key functional difference between ionotropic and metabotropic receptors?
quiz.answer: Ionotropic receptors are ligand-gated ion channels producing fast (millisecond) responses; metabotropic receptors act through G proteins and second messengers, giving slower, longer-lasting effects.

quiz.prompt: Why is the NMDA receptor described as a 'coincidence detector'?
quiz.answer: It opens only when glutamate is bound AND the postsynaptic cell is depolarized enough to expel its Mg²⁺ block, so it signals the coincidence of presynaptic input and postsynaptic activity — the substrate for Hebbian learning.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Neurotransmitters are the chemical messages neurons send. The receiving cell has "locks" — **receptors** — that only certain messengers fit. Some locks, when opened, instantly swing a door wide and let charged particles flood in. Other locks instead kick off a slower chain of events inside the cell. So the *same* gap can carry fast or slow signals depending on which lock the message lands on.

### Precisely

Common transmitters: **glutamate** (the main excitatory "go" signal), **GABA** and **glycine** (the main inhibitory "stop" signals), and modulators like **acetylcholine, dopamine, serotonin, norepinephrine**. Receptors come in two families. **Ionotropic** receptors (AMPA, NMDA, $\text{GABA}_A$) are *ligand-gated ion channels* — the messenger binds and the channel itself opens within milliseconds. **Metabotropic** receptors (mGluR; most dopamine and serotonin receptors) activate internal **G proteins** and **second messengers**, giving slower effects lasting hundreds of milliseconds to minutes.

### Worked example

Glutamate released at a synapse hits two receptor types on the same spine. **AMPA** receptors open instantly, letting $\text{Na}^+$ in for a fast EPSP. **NMDA** receptors are special: they bind glutamate *but stay blocked* by a magnesium ion ($\text{Mg}^{2+}$) lodged in the pore — until the cell is already depolarized enough to expel the $\text{Mg}^{2+}$. So NMDA only passes current when glutamate **and** postsynaptic depolarization happen *together*. It is a molecular **coincidence detector**.

### Why it's true / how it works

The crucial principle: a synapse's **sign** (excite vs inhibit) is set by the *receptor*, not the transmitter alone. Glutamate's channels admit positive ions (excitatory); GABA acting on $\text{GABA}_A$ opens chloride channels (usually inhibitory). The same molecule can do opposite things at different receptors. The slow metabotropic pathway, by contrast, doesn't open a channel directly — it launches a cascade that retunes the cell's excitability over a longer timescale.

### Where it connects

This atom refines the **chemical-synapse** into *how fast* and *which sign*. The NMDA coincidence detector is the molecular linchpin of **ltp-ltd** and therefore **hebbian-learning** and **stdp**. The slow metabotropic route is the basis of **neuromodulation**.

### Watch out

Two traps. First, "GABA = inhibition" is only *usually* true: in early development (and some adult cells) the chloride gradient is reversed, so $\text{GABA}_A$ can *excite*. Second, do not equate "neurotransmitter" with "excitatory" or "inhibitory" — that label belongs to the receptor and the ion it gates, not the molecule.

### Worth knowing

Termination matters as much as release: after acting, transmitter must be cleared from the cleft — by **reuptake transporters** (the target of many antidepressants and stimulants), by **enzymatic breakdown** (acetylcholinesterase chops up acetylcholine; nerve-agent toxins block exactly this), or by diffusion. Without fast clearance the signal would smear in time and the synapse could not transmit discrete events. It is also worth noting that a single neuron can release more than one transmitter (co-transmission), and that the *same* receptor family often comes in many subtypes with different kinetics and drug sensitivities — which is how pharmacology can selectively target, say, one GABA-A subtype for anxiety without shutting down all inhibition.

atoms.title: Synaptic integration & spatiotemporal summation
atoms.summary: A neuron decides to fire by summing many graded EPSPs and IPSPs across its dendrites in space and time.

depths.eli5: A neuron is constantly getting little nudges from thousands of other neurons — some pushing it toward firing, some pulling it back. It doesn't react to any single nudge; it adds them all up. If the running total at the trigger zone is big enough, the neuron fires a spike. That adding-up process is called synaptic integration.
depths.core: Each synapse produces only a small graded potential (a tiny voltage bump or dip); the neuron sums many of them. Spatial summation adds inputs arriving at different places on the cell at the same moment. Temporal summation adds inputs arriving at nearly the same place in quick succession — how 'quick' is set by the membrane time constant τ_m. Excitatory (toward-firing) and inhibitory (away-from-firing) inputs combine, and the net voltage at the axon initial segment (the trigger zone) decides whether the firing threshold is reached. One synapse alone is almost always far too weak to fire the cell.
depths.deep: This summation is not a plain straight-line addition. Dendrites have their own active machinery (such as local NMDA-receptor 'spikes' and other voltage-sensitive channels) that let a single dendritic branch behave like a mini-processor doing AND-like logic (fire only if several inputs land together). So one neuron can act like a small multi-layer network rather than a single adding point. Inhibition placed near the cell body can cancel ('shunt') excitation arriving from farther out (shunting inhibition). This is exactly where the cell's physical shape turns into computation.

quiz.answer: Spatial summation adds inputs from different locations arriving at the same time; temporal summation adds inputs at the same location arriving close together in time (within τ_m).
