atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

A neuron is constantly getting little nudges from thousands of other neurons — some pushing it toward firing, some pulling it back. It does not react to any single nudge; it *adds them all up*. If the running total at the trigger zone is big enough, the neuron fires a spike. That adding-up process is **synaptic integration**.

### Precisely

Each synapse produces only a small graded **postsynaptic potential** (a tiny voltage bump, EPSP, or dip, IPSP); the neuron sums many of them. **Spatial summation** adds inputs arriving at different places at the same instant. **Temporal summation** adds inputs at nearly the same place in quick succession — how "quick" is set by the membrane time constant $\tau_m$. Excitatory and inhibitory inputs combine, and the net voltage at the **axon initial segment** decides whether **threshold** is reached. One synapse alone is almost always far too weak.

### Worked example

Suppose one EPSP raises the soma by $0.3\,\text{mV}$ and threshold is $15\,\text{mV}$ above rest. A single input does nothing. But if $60$ excitatory synapses fire within one $\tau_m$ window (say $\sim 20\,\text{ms}$), their bumps overlap and sum toward $\sim 18\,\text{mV}$ — enough to fire. Now add one well-placed IPSP near the soma: by opening chloride channels it can "**shunt**" much of that excitation (lowering the membrane resistance so the EPSPs leak away), canceling inputs arriving from farther out and preventing the spike.

### Why it's true / how it works

Summation is *not* plain linear addition. Dendrites have active machinery — local **NMDA spikes** and other voltage-sensitive channels — that let a single branch behave like a mini-processor doing AND-like logic (fire only if several inputs land together). So one neuron can act like a small multilayer network rather than a single summing point. The cell's physical shape (from **passive-cable** $\lambda$ and $\tau_m$) is what turns wiring into computation.

### Where it connects

Integration sits on top of the **chemical-synapse** and **neurotransmitters-receptors** (the inputs) and the **passive-cable** (how they spread and decay). Its output is the **action-potential**; its abstraction is the weighted sum of the **perceptron**; its dendritic nonlinearities foreshadow **artificial-neural-networks**.

### Watch out

Don't picture the neuron as a perfect linear adder. Distant inputs are discounted (cable decay), inhibition can *divide* rather than just subtract (shunting), and dendritic branches can fire local spikes. Treating integration as simple arithmetic misses exactly where single-neuron computation gets interesting.

### Worth knowing

The *location* of a synapse on the dendritic tree changes its vote: inputs near the soma have large, fast effects, while distal inputs are filtered and delayed by the cable — yet neurons partly compensate with distance-dependent boosting of distal synapses ("dendritic democracy"). Timing interacts with place, too: a distal input that would be too weak alone can trigger a local **dendritic spike** if several arrive together, which then propagates to the soma as a large, sharply timed event. Inhibition's placement is equally strategic — inhibition on the *axon initial segment* can veto the cell's output entirely, while inhibition out on a branch only gates that branch. So the same number of synapses can compute very different functions depending purely on *where* they land.

atoms.title: Long-term potentiation & depression
atoms.summary: Synaptic strength can be persistently increased (LTP) or decreased (LTD) by patterns of activity — the cellular basis of memory.

depths.eli5: Synapses (the junctions between neurons) have an adjustable strength, like a volume dial. Use a connection a lot in the right pattern and the dial turns up and stays up — that lasting strengthening is called long-term potentiation, LTP. Use it the wrong way and the dial turns down — long-term depression, LTD. The brain learns and remembers largely by adjusting these dials, and the changes can last for years.
depths.core: At many glutamate-using ('glutamatergic') synapses, strong or precisely coincident activity strongly activates NMDA receptors, letting calcium (Ca²⁺) into the receiving cell's dendritic spine (a tiny bump where a synapse sits). That calcium triggers more AMPA receptors (the fast-acting glutamate receptors) to be inserted into the membrane, so the synapse responds more strongly from then on — that is LTP. A weaker but longer-lasting calcium signal does the opposite: it removes AMPA receptors, weakening the synapse — that is LTD. Both can last from hours to a lifetime, which is exactly what a lasting memory needs.
depths.deep: Calcium acts as a decision switch through its size and timing: a large, fast calcium rise activates an enzyme called CaMKII and produces LTP, while a modest, sustained rise activates opposing enzymes (phosphatases) and produces LTD (the basis of a 'sliding threshold' idea known as the BCM rule). Early LTP just shuffles existing receptors around; late, long-lasting LTP requires the cell to switch on genes and build new proteins, which get 'captured' at the synapses that were recently active (the synaptic tagging and capture idea). In short, LTP and LTD are the real-synapse machinery behind 'Hebbian learning.'

atoms.note: Calcium is the decision variable: a big fast rise → LTP (strengthen); a small sustained rise → LTD (weaken).

quiz.prompt: What postsynaptic event distinguishes LTP induction from LTD induction at glutamatergic synapses?
quiz.answer: A large, fast NMDA-mediated Ca²⁺ rise drives LTP (more AMPA receptors); a smaller, sustained Ca²⁺ rise drives LTD (fewer AMPA receptors).

quiz.prompt: Why does late-phase LTP, but not early LTP, require new protein synthesis?
quiz.answer: Early LTP is implemented by trafficking existing AMPA receptors; making the change persist for many hours requires gene transcription and new proteins, captured at tagged active synapses.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Synapses (the junctions between neurons) have an adjustable strength, like a volume dial. Use a connection a lot in the right pattern and the dial turns *up* and stays up — that lasting strengthening is **long-term potentiation (LTP)**. Use it the wrong way and the dial turns *down* — **long-term depression (LTD)**. The brain learns and remembers largely by adjusting these dials, and the changes can last for years.

### Precisely

At many glutamate-using (**glutamatergic**) synapses, strong or precisely coincident activity strongly activates **NMDA receptors**, letting **calcium** ($\text{Ca}^{2+}$) into the **dendritic spine** (the tiny bump where the synapse sits). A **large, fast** calcium rise drives more **AMPA receptors** into the membrane, so the synapse responds more strongly thereafter — **LTP**. A **smaller, sustained** calcium signal does the opposite, removing AMPA receptors — **LTD**. Both can last from hours to a lifetime.

### Worked example

Apply a classic LTP protocol: a brief high-frequency tetanus ($\sim 100\,\text{Hz}$) to the input pathway. The strong depolarization expels the $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ block from NMDA receptors, glutamate is present, so NMDA channels open and admit a *sharp* calcium spike. That spike activates the enzyme **CaMKII**, which drives AMPA-receptor insertion. Test the synapse minutes later with a single pulse: the EPSP is now markedly larger — and stays larger for hours. Swap the protocol for prolonged *low*-frequency stimulation ($\sim 1\,\text{Hz}$): calcium rises modestly but persistently, activating opposing **phosphatases** that *remove* AMPA receptors — LTD.

### Why it's true / how it works

Calcium acts as a **decision switch** through its *amplitude and timing*: a big fast rise $\to$ CaMKII $\to$ LTP; a modest sustained rise $\to$ phosphatases $\to$ LTD (the "sliding threshold" of the **BCM** rule). Early LTP just shuffles existing receptors; **late** LTP requires switching on genes and building new proteins, captured at recently active synapses (**synaptic tagging and capture**).

### Where it connects

LTP/LTD are the real-synapse machinery behind **hebbian-learning** and **stdp**, the cellular basis of **hippocampus-memory**, and a step in **memory-consolidation**. The NMDA coincidence detector comes from **neurotransmitters-receptors**.

### Watch out

The common error is "more activity always strengthens." Not so — it is the *calcium signal's shape* that decides direction, so the very same synapse can be potentiated or depressed depending on the pattern. And LTP in a dish is a *model* of memory, not memory itself; the link to behavioral remembering is strong but inferential.

### Worth knowing

LTP famously satisfies the criteria you would *want* of a memory mechanism — it is **input-specific** (only the stimulated synapses strengthen, not the whole cell), **associative** (a weak input can be potentiated if paired with a strong one nearby), and **long-lasting** — and these three properties map directly onto the cellular requirements for **hebbian-learning**. Structurally, strong LTP enlarges the dendritic spine and can even split one synapse into two, so learning physically *reshapes* the connection, not just its gain. A subtlety worth holding onto: blocking NMDA receptors blocks *induction* of LTP but not its *expression* once established, which is how researchers showed the calcium trigger and the maintained change are separable steps.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Here is the brain's simplest learning rule in plain words: if neuron A keeps helping neuron B fire, the connection from A to B gets stronger. The catchphrase is "**neurons that fire together, wire together.**" Connections that reliably help cause activity get reinforced, so the brain gradually wires up the patterns it keeps seeing.

### Precisely

Donald Hebb's 1949 postulate: when neuron A repeatedly takes part in firing neuron B, the synapse A$\to$B strengthens. In its simplest mathematical form, the change in the connection strength (the **weight** $w$) is proportional to the product of the input activity $x$ and the output activity $y$:

$$\Delta w \propto x\,y.$$

Two features matter: the rule is **local** (each synapse uses only signals available right at it) and **correlation-based** (it responds to pre- and postsynaptic activity occurring *together*). This is the conceptual root of **unsupervised** learning — finding structure in data with no answer key.

### Worked example

Train a single unit with two inputs. Whenever input $x_1$ is active, the unit fires ($y=1$); input $x_2$ is usually silent. Apply $\Delta w \propto x\,y$ repeatedly: $w_1$ grows every time $x_1$ and $y$ coincide, while $w_2$ barely moves (since $x_2$ and $y$ rarely co-occur). After many trials the unit responds strongly to $x_1$ — it has *learned* the input that reliably accompanies its firing. But notice a problem: as $w_1$ grows, the unit fires even more for $x_1$, which grows $w_1$ further — the weight runs away.

### Why it's true / how it works

Pure Hebbian strengthening is **unstable**: strong synapses fire the cell more, strengthening themselves further, so weights blow up to infinity. Real systems fix this with **normalization** (bound the total weight) or a **sliding threshold** (the **BCM** rule) that subtracts an activity-dependent term, letting weights *also weaken* and producing useful selectivity — like neurons preferring one eye (ocular dominance) or one edge orientation. The clean biological implementation is NMDA-dependent **ltp-ltd**, which strengthens a synapse only when input and output coincide — exactly Hebb's condition.

### Where it connects

Hebbian learning is the abstraction of **ltp-ltd**, the parent of **stdp** (timing-precise Hebb), and the ancestor of unsupervised learning in **artificial-neural-networks**. Its error-driven cousin is the **perceptron** rule.

### Watch out

"Fire together, wire together" is catchy but *incomplete*: without a weakening term or normalization, Hebbian weights diverge. Also, raw correlation is not causation — pure Hebb strengthens *any* co-active pair; STDP's timing requirement is what adds a sense of "A may have *caused* B.\"

### Worth knowing

A clarifying mathematical fact: a Hebbian unit with a normalization constraint tends to extract the leading **principal component** of its inputs — the single direction of greatest variance — which is why pure Hebbian learning is naturally a *feature-discovery* / dimensionality-reduction rule (Oja's rule makes this exact and stable). This is the precise sense in which "fire together, wire together" performs *unsupervised* learning: it finds the dominant structure in the input stream with no teacher. Adding lateral inhibition between several Hebbian units forces them to capture *different* components, yielding a small set of complementary feature detectors — the same trick that, scaled up, lets unsupervised networks learn edge-detector-like filters resembling the **receptive-fields** of early visual cortex.

atoms.title: Spike-timing-dependent plasticity
atoms.summary: The sign and size of synaptic change depend on the millisecond timing between pre- and postsynaptic spikes.

depths.eli5: This is Hebbian learning sharpened to the millisecond. Whether a connection grows stronger or weaker depends on the exact order of two spikes: if the input neuron fires just BEFORE the receiving neuron does, the link strengthens; if it fires just AFTER, the link weakens. The order — within a few thousandths of a second — decides which way the dial turns.
depths.core: Spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) is a time-precise version of Hebbian learning. When the presynaptic (sending) spike comes a few milliseconds before the postsynaptic (receiving) spike, the synapse strengthens (LTP); when it comes after, the synapse weakens (LTD). Guo-qiang Bi and Mu-ming Poo (1998) measured the 'STDP window': the amount of strengthening or weakening falls off exponentially as the spike-time gap Δt (the difference between the two spike times) grows, with characteristic time scales of roughly 10–20 ms and essentially no effect once the gap exceeds about 40–100 ms.
depths.deep: The asymmetry of the window implements causal inference — figuring out what causes what. Inputs that help cause a spike (they arrive just before) are strengthened; inputs that arrive too late to have helped are weakened. So a neuron tuned by STDP comes to favor inputs that predict its own firing, and the network can learn ordered sequences and predictive relationships. Mechanistically STDP rides on NMDA-receptor coincidence detection plus the 'back-propagating action potential' — a copy of the output spike that travels backward into the dendrites to announce 'I just fired,' so each synapse can compare its input timing against the cell's output. STDP is a leading model for how networks self-organize with no external teacher.

atoms.note: Pre-before-post → strengthen (the input may have caused the spike); post-before-pre → weaken. The window is only tens of milliseconds wide.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

This is Hebbian learning sharpened to the millisecond. Whether a connection grows stronger or weaker depends on the exact *order* of two spikes: if the input neuron fires just **before** the receiving neuron does, the link strengthens; if it fires just **after**, the link weakens. The order — within a few thousandths of a second — decides which way the dial turns.

### Precisely

**Spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP)** makes Hebbian learning time-precise. Let $\Delta t = t_{post} - t_{pre}$ be the gap between the postsynaptic and presynaptic spike times. When the presynaptic spike comes a few milliseconds *before* the postsynaptic one ($\Delta t > 0$, small), the synapse **strengthens** (LTP); when it comes *after* ($\Delta t < 0$), it **weakens** (LTD). The amount falls off exponentially with $|\Delta t|$, with time constants of roughly $10$–$20\,\text{ms}$ and essentially no effect once $|\Delta t|$ exceeds $\sim 40$–$100\,\text{ms}$.

### Worked example

Pair a presynaptic spike at $t=0$ with a postsynaptic spike at $t=+10\,\text{ms}$ (pre leads post by $10\,\text{ms}$). Because the input arrived just *before* the output — and could plausibly have helped cause it — the synapse is potentiated; the strengthening is sizable but a bit less than for a $2\,\text{ms}$ gap (exponential decay). Now flip the order: post at $t=0$, pre at $t=+10\,\text{ms}$. The input arrived *too late* to have helped, so the synapse is depressed. Bi and Poo (1998) measured exactly this asymmetric window.

### Why it's true / how it works

The window's asymmetry implements **causal inference**: inputs that help *cause* a spike are strengthened; inputs arriving too late are weakened. Mechanistically STDP rides on NMDA-receptor coincidence detection (from **neurotransmitters-receptors**) plus the **back-propagating action potential** — a copy of the output spike that travels *backward* into the dendrites to announce "I just fired," so each synapse can compare its input timing against the cell's output.

### Where it connects

STDP is the timing-precise form of **hebbian-learning** and a concrete reading-out of **ltp-ltd**. It lets networks learn ordered sequences and predictive relations, links to **neural-oscillations** (phase sets which pairings get strengthened), and is a candidate biological route toward the credit assignment problem in **artificial-neural-networks**.

### Watch out

The canonical pre-before-post-strengthens window is *not universal* — some synapses show the opposite or symmetric windows, and the rule depends on firing rate and dendritic location. Treat the classic curve as the prototype, not a law that holds identically everywhere.

### Worth knowing

STDP turns a network into a **sequence learner**: if neurons fire in a repeated order A$\to$B$\to$C, the forward links (A$\to$B, B$\to$C) are strengthened while the backward links are weakened, so the network learns to *predict and replay* the sequence. This is one proposed substrate for how the brain anticipates the next step in a familiar routine. The rule also self-limits run-away growth that pure Hebb suffers from, because a synapse that grows too strong starts to *advance* the postsynaptic spike to *before* its own input, flipping it into the depression regime — a built-in stabilizing feedback. As with rate-based Hebb, real STDP additionally depends on firing rate, dendritic location, and neuromodulatory state, so the textbook two-lobed window is a clean idealization of a richer rule.

atoms.title: Neural coding: rate vs temporal codes
atoms.summary: Information can be carried by how fast neurons fire (rate code) or by the precise timing of individual spikes (temporal code).

It can fire more spikes per second (a 'rate code' — more spikes means a stronger signal). Or it can carry meaning in the exact timing and rhythm of its spikes (a 'temporal code' — when each spike lands matters). Both carry information, and the brain uses each in different places.

It's robust to noise but slow, and it throws away the fine detail of individual spike times. A temporal code instead uses the precise timing — or the relative latency (which neuron fired first) — of spikes; it can pack more information into each spike and react faster. Real neurons often use both: a rate code for slowly changing signals, and timing (for example, the phase of a spike relative to an ongoing brain rhythm) for fast or relational information.

Temporal codes are information-dense but demand precise, reliable spiking and timing-sensitive readers such as coincidence detectors (cells that fire only when inputs arrive together). Examples of timing-based codes include hippocampal 'theta phase precession' (a spike's phase within a rhythm shifts to encode position) and first-spike-latency codes (the first cell to fire signals the strongest input) — both show the brain exploiting timing when speed or capacity demand it.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Since every spike is the *same size* (all-or-none), a neuron cannot shout "louder." So how does it say how strong something is? Two ways. It can fire **more spikes per second** (a *rate code* — more spikes means a stronger signal). Or it can carry meaning in the **exact timing** of its spikes (a *temporal code* — *when* each spike lands matters). Both carry information; the brain uses each in different places.

### Precisely

A **rate code** represents a stimulus by the average firing rate (spikes per second) over a time window. It is robust to noise but slow, and it discards fine spike-timing detail. A **temporal code** uses the precise timing — or the relative *latency* (which neuron fired first) — of spikes; it can pack more information into each spike and react faster. Real neurons often use both: rate for slowly changing signals, timing (e.g., spike **phase** relative to an ongoing rhythm) for fast or relational information.

### Worked example

A motion-sensitive neuron prefers rightward motion. Show slow rightward drift and it fires $\sim 20$ spikes/s; faster drift, $\sim 60$ spikes/s — a clean *rate* code you can read by counting spikes over $\sim 100\,\text{ms}$. Now consider sound localization: a click reaches your left ear $\sim 0.3\,\text{ms}$ before your right. Neurons exploit *which input arrived first*, encoding direction in spike *timing* differences far finer than any rate could carry in the few milliseconds available. Same currency (spikes), two readout strategies.

### Why it's true / how it works

Which code is used is constrained by **reliability** and by **what reads the signal downstream**. Rate codes need integration time but tolerate jitter (noisy spike times). Temporal codes are information-dense but demand precise, reliable spiking and timing-sensitive readers — **coincidence detectors** that fire only when inputs arrive together. Examples: hippocampal **theta phase precession** (a spike's phase within a rhythm encodes position) and first-spike-latency codes.

### Where it connects

Coding rests on the all-or-none **action-potential** (why amplitude carries nothing) and feeds **population-coding** (many cells together). Temporal codes lean on **neural-oscillations** (phase as a clock) and on coincidence-detecting **neurotransmitters-receptors** (NMDA). It is the substrate decoded by **brain-computer-interfaces**.

### Watch out

"Rate vs temporal" is not a strict either/or — it depends on the time window you average over and on what the downstream neuron is built to read. A code that looks like "rate" over $200\,\text{ms}$ may carry precise timing information on a finer scale. The honest answer is usually "both, at different scales.\"

### Worth knowing

A key concept for distinguishing the two coding schemes is **reliability**: if a neuron's spike *times* repeat precisely across identical stimulus presentations, timing can carry information; if only the *count* is stable while individual times jitter, the usable code is rate. Real cortex sits in between, and the answer often depends on the *behavioral timescale* — a fast reflex cannot wait to average a rate, so it must read the first spikes, whereas a slow perceptual judgment can integrate counts. Information theory makes this quantitative: by measuring how much *mutual information* a spike train carries about the stimulus under each assumption, one can ask directly how much extra information precise timing adds over rate alone — and for many sensory neurons, the answer is a substantial amount.

atoms.title: Population & distributed coding
atoms.summary: Many noisy neurons together represent a variable more accurately than any single cell, often via overlapping tuning curves.

depths.eli5: Any single neuron is a noisy, unreliable guesser. But if you have a whole crowd of neurons, each tuned to prefer a slightly different thing, you can take a vote and the average comes out sharp and accurate — like polling many people instead of asking one. So meaning lives in the pattern of activity across many cells, not in any one cell by itself.
depths.core: Population coding represents a stimulus using the combined activity of many neurons, each with its own tuning curve — a graph showing which value it responds to most (its preferred direction, edge orientation, sound frequency, and so on). Because each cell's noise is largely its own, averaging across the population cancels that noise out. A simple readout like a 'population vector,' or a statistical best-guess method (maximum-likelihood decoding), can then recover the encoded value far more precisely than any single cell could. Spreading the code across many cells also makes it robust: losing a few neurons barely hurts.
depths.deep: Apostolos Georgopoulos's population-vector work showed the motor cortex encodes the direction of an arm movement as the vector sum of many cells' preferred directions, each weighted by how hard it is firing. More generally, how well you can decode a population depends on the structure of its correlated noise — noise patterns that look like the signal limit the information available, while noise patterns pointing in unrelated directions do not. Real brains use 'sparse, distributed' codes (a modest fraction of cells active for any item) that balance capacity, energy cost, and ease of decoding — which is why the brain uses neither single 'grandmother cells' (one cell per concept) nor fully dense codes.

atoms.note: The population vector: each neuron 'votes' along its preferred stimulus, weighted by its firing rate; the vector sum of all those votes is the estimate.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Any single neuron is a noisy, unreliable guesser. But with a *crowd* of neurons — each tuned to prefer a slightly different thing — you can take a vote and the average comes out sharp and accurate, like polling many people instead of asking one. Meaning lives in the *pattern of activity across many cells*, not in any single cell.

### Precisely

**Population coding** represents a stimulus using the combined activity of many neurons, each with its own **tuning curve** — a graph of how strongly it responds across stimulus values (its preferred direction, edge orientation, sound frequency, etc.). Because each cell's noise is largely independent, averaging across the population cancels it. A simple readout — a **population vector**, or **maximum-likelihood decoding** — then recovers the encoded value far more precisely than any single cell could.

### Worked example

Georgopoulos studied motor cortex during arm reaches. Each neuron fires most for one **preferred direction** and less for others (a broad cosine-like tuning curve). To estimate the *actual* reach direction, give each neuron a vector pointing along its preferred direction, scaled by its current firing rate, and **sum** all those vectors. Individually the cells are broadly tuned and noisy, but the **population vector** — the weighted sum — points accurately in the true movement direction. Lose a handful of neurons and the estimate barely changes: the code is robust.

### Why it's true / how it works

Averaging $N$ roughly independent noisy estimates shrinks the noise by about $\sqrt{N}$, so a population is far sharper than one cell. *How well* you can decode depends on the **structure of correlated noise**: noise patterns that mimic the signal limit information, while noise in unrelated directions does not. Real brains use **sparse, distributed** codes (a modest fraction of cells active per item) balancing capacity, energy, and decodability.

### Where it connects

Population coding builds on single-cell **neural-coding** and **receptive-fields** (tuning curves) and underlies **hierarchical-processing**, **motor-control** (population dynamics), and the readout decoded by **brain-computer-interfaces**.

### Watch out

The brain uses neither extreme: not single "**grandmother cells**" (one cell per concept) nor fully dense codes. And the population vector assumes roughly *uniform, independent* tuning — when noise is strongly correlated with the signal, naive averaging *overestimates* how much information is there. Correlations, not just cell count, set the real precision.

### Worth knowing

Sparseness is a deliberate engineering choice with measurable benefits: a code where only a small fraction of cells fire for any item costs less energy (spikes are expensive), reduces overlap between memories (helping the pattern separation of **hippocampus-memory**), and is easier to read out linearly. The flip side is capacity — too sparse and you cannot represent enough distinct items — so the brain lands on an intermediate, *sparse-but-distributed* regime. Decoding such codes also depends on the *readout* a downstream neuron can actually implement: a single neuron computes a weighted sum (a linear decoder), so codes that are *linearly* decodable are biologically privileged, which is one reason overlapping tuning curves are so common.

atoms.title: Neural circuits: excitation, inhibition & motifs
atoms.summary: Neurons wire into recurring circuit motifs — feedforward and feedback inhibition, lateral inhibition, recurrence — that perform stereotyped computations.

depths.eli5: Neurons don't connect at random; they wire up in a handful of repeating little patterns, like reusable Lego shapes. Each pattern does a specific job — sharpening a signal, keeping the overall activity from going wild, or holding onto a piece of information. Build a brain out of these few building blocks and you get all its different functions.
depths.core: Circuits are assembled from a few recurring wiring patterns ('motifs'). Feedforward inhibition (an input excites a target and also, slightly later, an inhibitory cell that quiets that target) creates precise timing windows. Feedback (recurrent) inhibition (active cells switch on inhibitory neighbors that calm them) stabilizes and normalizes activity. Lateral inhibition (active cells suppress their neighbors) sharpens contrast. Recurrent excitation (cells that re-excite each other) can sustain activity to hold a memory or amplify a weak input. Keeping excitation and inhibition roughly matched — the 'E/I balance' — keeps a network sensitive and responsive instead of either silent or saturated (maxed out).
depths.deep: Inhibition is far more than an off switch. It can implement division (turning a signal down by a factor — gain control or 'normalization'), gate whether information passes, help generate rhythmic oscillations, and produce winner-take-all dynamics (one option suppresses the rest until a single winner remains). Tight E/I balance yields irregular, unsynchronized firing that is both energy-efficient and quick to respond, plausibly keeping the network near a 'critical point' (a finely poised regime, explored in a later atom). These motifs are the brain's reusable subroutines, appearing everywhere from the retina to the cortex.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Neurons do not connect at random; they wire up in a handful of repeating little patterns, like reusable Lego shapes. Each pattern does a specific job — sharpening a signal, keeping overall activity from running wild, or holding onto a piece of information. Build a brain from these few building blocks and you get its many functions.

### Precisely

Circuits are assembled from recurring wiring **motifs**. **Feedforward inhibition** (an input excites a target *and*, slightly later, an inhibitory cell that quiets it) creates precise timing windows. **Feedback (recurrent) inhibition** (active cells switch on inhibitory neighbors that calm them) stabilizes and normalizes activity. **Lateral inhibition** (active cells suppress their neighbors) sharpens contrast. **Recurrent excitation** (cells re-exciting each other) can sustain activity to hold a memory or amplify a weak input. Keeping excitation and inhibition roughly matched — the **E/I balance** — keeps a network responsive instead of silent or saturated.

### Worked example

Take lateral inhibition in the retina. A bright edge crosses a patch of photoreceptors. Cells looking at the bright side fire hard and, via lateral connections, *suppress* their neighbors on the dim side. The result: responses are *exaggerated* right at the boundary — the bright side looks brighter and the dark side darker near the edge. The circuit has computed an *edge* (local contrast) rather than reporting raw light level. This is the same operation a center-surround **receptive-field** performs.

### Why it's true / how it works

Inhibition is far more than an off switch. It can implement **division** (divisive normalization / gain control — turning a signal down by a *factor*), **gate** whether information passes, generate **oscillations**, and produce **winner-take-all** dynamics (one option suppresses the rest until a single winner remains). Tight E/I balance yields irregular, energy-efficient firing that responds quickly and may keep the network near a critical point.

### Where it connects

These motifs build on **synaptic-integration** and the **electrical-synapse** (synchrony). Lateral inhibition shapes **receptive-fields**; recurrent excitation underlies **working-memory**; E/I balance feeds **neural-oscillations** and **neural-criticality**; gain control links to **attention**.

### Watch out

Do not treat inhibition as merely "negative excitation." Subtractive inhibition shifts a response *down*; **divisive** (shunting) inhibition scales it by a factor — very different computations. And "balance" does not mean equal-and-opposite cancellation to zero; it means *tracking* excitation closely enough to keep firing controlled and fast, not silent.

### Worth knowing

A useful way to see why these motifs recur is that each maps onto a basic *operation*: feedforward inhibition implements a temporal **derivative / coincidence window**, feedback inhibition implements **negative feedback / stabilization**, lateral inhibition implements **spatial sharpening / contrast**, and recurrent excitation implements **integration / memory**. Real cortical microcircuits stack several of these in the canonical six-layer pattern, reused across the whole cortex with only modest variation — which is part of why one cortical area can, in principle, be repurposed for a different sense. The interneurons doing the inhibition are themselves diverse (distinct types target the soma, the dendrites, or other interneurons), and which inhibitory cell is engaged determines *whether* the circuit gates, normalizes, or times.

atoms.title: Working memory & persistent activity
atoms.summary: Holding information in mind for seconds may be implemented by recurrent excitation that sustains activity after a stimulus is gone.

depths.eli5: Working memory is your mental scratchpad — the way you hold a phone number in mind for a few seconds while you dial. One way the brain does this: a group of neurons keeps firing on its own even after the thing you heard is gone, like an echo the brain deliberately keeps going so the information doesn't vanish.
depths.core: Working memory is the short-term, active holding and manipulation of information — the prefrontal cortex (the front of the brain) acting like a mental sketchpad. A classic mechanism is persistent neuronal activity: during the 'delay' part of a memory task (after the cue disappears, before you respond), certain prefrontal neurons keep firing for the remembered item even though nothing is on screen. Loops of recurrent excitation (neurons re-exciting each other), held in check by inhibition, settle into self-sustaining states called attractors that keep the memory alive. The catch: that same self-feeding activity is also what makes the memory easy to knock off course with a distraction.
depths.deep: Attractor-network models picture this as a stable 'bump' of activity in a recurrent network — a continuous attractor for analog quantities (like a remembered angle) or discrete attractors for distinct categories — tuned near a tipping point (a bifurcation) so a brief input can flip the state on or off. Newer evidence suggests information can also be stored 'activity-silent' — held in fleeting short-term synaptic changes rather than ongoing firing, and reawakened only when probed — so persistent firing may be just one of several mechanisms. Working memory is the bridge from circuit dynamics up to cognition, and many theories treat it as the gateway to conscious access.

atoms.note: Persistent delay-period firing in prefrontal cortex is the classic mechanism; 'activity-silent' synaptic traces are a newer, complementary one.

quiz.answer: Recurrent excitation balanced by inhibition forms stable activity states (attractors) that persist without input; the tradeoff is that the same recurrence makes the held state susceptible to distractor inputs and drift.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Working memory is your mental scratchpad — how you hold a phone number in mind for a few seconds while you dial. One way the brain does it: a group of neurons keeps firing on its own *even after* the thing you heard is gone, like an echo the brain deliberately keeps going so the information does not vanish.

### Precisely

**Working memory** is the short-term active holding and manipulation of information — classically tied to the **prefrontal cortex** acting like a sketchpad. A central mechanism is **persistent neuronal activity**: during the **delay period** of a memory task (after the cue disappears, before the response), certain neurons keep firing for the remembered item even with nothing on screen. Loops of **recurrent excitation**, held in check by inhibition, settle into self-sustaining states called **attractors** that keep the memory alive.

### Worked example

In a classic delayed-response task, a monkey sees a cue flash at one location, then a blank delay of several seconds, then must look back to the remembered spot. Record from prefrontal cortex during the delay: a subset of neurons tuned to that location *keep firing the whole time*, even though the cue is gone. Different cues activate different neuron groups. The persistent firing *is* the held memory — and if a distractor flashes during the delay, it can knock the activity off, and the animal forgets, revealing the memory's fragility.

### Why it's true / how it works

**Attractor-network** models picture this as a stable "bump" of activity in a recurrent network — a *continuous* attractor for analog quantities (a remembered angle) or *discrete* attractors for categories — poised near a tipping point (**bifurcation**) so a brief input can switch the state on or off. Newer evidence suggests information can also be stored "**activity-silent**," in fleeting short-term synaptic changes rather than ongoing firing, and reawakened only when probed — so persistent firing may be one mechanism among several.

### Where it connects

Working memory builds directly on the recurrent-excitation motif of **neural-circuits** and on **synaptic-integration**. Its attractor dynamics tie to **neuronal-dynamics** (bifurcations) and **neural-oscillations** (rhythms can multiplex several items). Many theories treat it as the gateway to conscious access (see **theories-of-consciousness**).

### Watch out

Persistent delay-period firing is the classic — but not the *only* — mechanism; "activity-silent" synaptic storage is a real complement, so do not assume a memory must be continuously "lit up" to be held. And the same recurrence that sustains a memory is exactly what makes it vulnerable to distraction and drift — stability and fragility are two faces of one mechanism.

### Worth knowing

Working memory has a famously small **capacity** — only a few items at once — and a leading idea ties this limit to the attractor dynamics: each held item is a separate self-sustaining activity bump, and too many bumps competing for shared recurrent circuitry destabilize one another. Oscillations may help pack items in: a **theta–gamma** scheme proposes each item occupies a distinct gamma cycle nested within a slower theta cycle, so the number of gamma cycles that fit sets the capacity. This connects working memory to **neural-oscillations** and explains why it is both powerful (active, manipulable) and fragile (limited, distractible) — the very recurrence that holds information also caps how much can be held and how well it resists interference.

atoms.title: Sensory transduction
atoms.summary: Receptor cells convert physical stimuli — light, sound, pressure, chemicals — into graded electrical signals.

depths.eli5: Your senses are translators that turn things in the world into electricity the brain can read. The eye turns light into electrical signals, the ear turns sound vibrations into them, the skin turns pressure into them. The brain never touches light or sound directly — everything it knows arrives as voltage. That translation step is called sensory transduction.
depths.core: Each sense has its own special machinery that converts a stimulus into the opening or closing of ion channels (those protein pores again). In vision, light hits photoreceptor cells (rods and cones) and sets off a chemical relay chain (a 'G-protein cascade': the light-sensing pigment rhodopsin activates a relay protein, transducin, then an enzyme, PDE, which lowers a small signaling molecule called cGMP, which closes channels). In hearing, hair cells in the cochlea (the inner ear's coiled tube) have tiny hairs (stereocilia) that, when bent by sound vibrations, mechanically yank channels open. Touch and smell receptors open channels by force or by a molecule binding. In every case the output is a graded receptor potential — a voltage whose size tracks how strong the stimulus is.
depths.deep: The transduction step sets the sensitivity and 'dynamic range' (the span from faintest to strongest detectable) of each sense. Vision's multi-step chemical cascade provides enormous amplification — a single photon can produce a measurable electrical current — but takes time, so it is slow. Hearing's mechanical gating is direct and microsecond-fast, which is what lets you locate sounds by the tiny timing difference between your two ears. Built-in adaptation at the transduction step (often via calcium feedback) lets receptors keep working across a vast range of intensities, from a dim star to bright sunlight.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Your senses are *translators* that turn things in the world into electricity the brain can read. The eye turns light into electrical signals, the ear turns sound vibrations into them, the skin turns pressure into them. The brain never touches light or sound directly — everything it knows arrives as voltage. That translation step is **sensory transduction**.

### Precisely

Each sense has dedicated machinery that converts a physical stimulus into the opening or closing of **ion channels**. In **vision**, light strikes **photoreceptors** (rods and cones) and sets off a G-protein cascade: the pigment **rhodopsin** activates the relay protein **transducin**, then the enzyme **PDE**, which lowers the messenger **cGMP**, which *closes* channels. In **hearing**, **hair cells** in the cochlea have tiny hairs (**stereocilia**) that, bent by sound vibration, *mechanically yank channels open*. Touch and smell open channels by force or by molecular binding. The output in every case is a graded **receptor potential** whose size tracks stimulus strength.

### Worked example

Track a single photon. It isomerizes one rhodopsin molecule. That one activated rhodopsin switches on *many* transducin molecules; each activates PDE; each PDE breaks down *many* cGMP molecules. cGMP normally holds channels open, so its fall lets channels *close*, reducing inward current — a measurable voltage change from *one photon*, thanks to multi-stage chemical amplification. Contrast hearing: a sound wave bends the stereocilia and pulls open channels *directly* via tiny "tip links," with no cascade — fast enough to track the microsecond timing your brain uses to localize sound.

### Why it's true / how it works

The transduction step sets each sense's **sensitivity** and **dynamic range** (faintest to strongest detectable). Vision's multi-step cascade gives enormous gain (single-photon detection) but is *slow*. Hearing's direct mechanical gating is *microsecond-fast* but lower-gain. Built-in **adaptation** (often via calcium feedback) lets receptors keep working from a dim star to bright sunlight.

### Where it connects

Transduction produces the graded potentials that **voltage-gated-channels** later convert into spikes, feeding **receptive-fields** and **hierarchical-processing**. The amplification logic reuses the metabotropic machinery of **neurotransmitters-receptors**.

### Watch out

A counterintuitive fact: vertebrate photoreceptors *hyperpolarize* (and *reduce* transmitter release) in response to light — they are most active in the *dark*. So "more stimulus $\to$ more firing" is not universal at the transduction stage; the sign depends on the specific cascade.

### Worth knowing

Adaptation deserves emphasis because it is what makes a fixed-range detector usable across an enormous span of intensities: photoreceptors recalibrate via calcium feedback so the *same* cells work from starlight to noon sunlight (about ten orders of magnitude of light), and hair cells adjust their channel tension to track ongoing sound. A second theme is **labeled lines**: each receptor type reports only its own modality, so the brain learns "this input means light" purely from *which* nerve fibers are active, not from any intrinsic difference in the spikes — stimulate the optic nerve electrically and you see flashes, not feel touch. This is why transduction is the irreversible commitment point: once a stimulus is converted to a receptor potential on a particular line, the brain treats it as that modality.

atoms.title: Receptive fields
atoms.summary: A sensory neuron responds only to stimuli in a specific region and pattern — its receptive field — built by circuit wiring.

depths.eli5: Each sensory neuron is picky. It has a favorite spot in the world (a particular patch of your visual field, say) and a favorite kind of pattern there. Show it the right thing in the right place and it fires hard; show it anything else and it stays quiet. That favorite spot-and-pattern is the neuron's 'receptive field.'
depths.core: A receptive field is the region of sensory space — plus the specific pattern within it — that makes a neuron respond. In vision, retinal ganglion cells and cells in the LGN (the lateral geniculate nucleus, a relay station between eye and cortex) have 'center-surround' fields: a small central spot that excites and a ring around it that inhibits (built by lateral inhibition), so the cell detects local contrast rather than uniform light. David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel showed that neurons in the primary visual cortex have oriented receptive fields — 'simple cells' fire best for an edge or bar at a particular angle and position, built by lining up several center-surround inputs in a row.
depths.deep: Receptive fields are effectively the brain's feature detectors. A center-surround field behaves like an edge/contrast filter (mathematically similar to a Laplacian operator); an oriented simple-cell field resembles a 'Gabor function,' which happens to be an efficient, sparse way to encode the statistics of natural images. The step from center-surround (spots) to oriented edges is the first rung of a processing hierarchy — and it is essentially the same operation that the first layers of a convolutional neural network learn to perform, one of the clearest links between brains and modern AI vision.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Each sensory neuron is picky. It has a favorite spot in the world (a particular patch of your visual field, say) and a favorite *kind of pattern* there. Show it the right thing in the right place and it fires hard; show it anything else and it stays quiet. That favorite spot-and-pattern is the neuron's **receptive field**.

### Precisely

A **receptive field** is the region of sensory space — plus the specific pattern within it — that drives a neuron. In vision, retinal ganglion cells and **LGN** (lateral geniculate nucleus) cells have **center-surround** fields: a small central spot that excites and a surrounding ring that inhibits (built by **lateral inhibition**), so the cell detects *local contrast* rather than uniform light. Hubel and Wiesel showed **primary visual cortex** neurons have *oriented* fields — "**simple cells**" fire best for an edge or bar at a particular angle and position.

### Worked example

Shine a small spot of light on a center-surround cell's center: it fires strongly. Now enlarge the spot to also cover the inhibitory surround: firing *drops*, because center excitation and surround inhibition cancel. Uniform light over the whole field barely moves the cell — it signals *contrast*, not brightness. Next, Hubel and Wiesel found that lining up several such center-surround inputs *in a row* yields a cortical simple cell that fires best for a bar oriented along that row, at that location — an **edge detector** built from spot detectors.

### Why it's true / how it works

Receptive fields are the brain's **feature detectors**. A center-surround field acts like a contrast/edge filter (mathematically akin to a *Laplacian*); an oriented simple-cell field resembles a **Gabor function**, which is an efficient, sparse way to encode natural-image statistics. The step from spots to oriented edges is the first rung of a processing hierarchy — essentially the same operation the first layers of a **convolutional neural network** learn.

### Where it connects

Receptive fields rest on **sensory-transduction** (the raw input) and the lateral-inhibition motif of **neural-circuits**. They are the unit of **population-coding** (overlapping tuning curves) and the first stage of **hierarchical-processing**, and they are the clearest biological parallel to **artificial-neural-networks**.

### Watch out

A receptive field is not just a *location* — it is location *plus preferred pattern*. Two cells can share the same patch of visual space yet have completely different fields (one prefers a vertical edge, the other horizontal). Reducing "receptive field" to "the spot it watches" throws away the feature-selectivity that is the whole point.

### Worth knowing

Receptive fields are not static — they *adapt* to context and learning. Surround suppression, attention, and the recent stimulus history can reshape a cell's effective field within seconds, so the "filter" is dynamic, not a fixed stencil. Hubel and Wiesel also distinguished **simple cells** (which care about the exact *position* of an oriented edge within their field) from **complex cells** (which respond to that orientation *anywhere* in the field) — the first concrete instance of the selectivity-then-invariance pairing that **hierarchical-processing** generalizes. Their critical-period experiments further showed that normal visual experience is *required* to wire these fields up properly, demonstrating that the feature detectors are shaped by activity-dependent plasticity, not hard-coded alone — a direct bridge to **hebbian-learning**.

atoms.title: Hierarchical sensory processing
atoms.summary: Sensory systems build increasingly abstract representations through successive stages, each pooling simpler features into more complex ones.

depths.eli5: Vision is built up in stages, like an assembly line. The first stage sees tiny edges. The next combines edges into corners and textures. The next builds shapes. The last recognizes whole objects and faces. Each stage takes the pieces found by the stage before it and assembles bigger, more meaningful pieces.
depths.core: Along the brain's visual 'ventral stream' — a chain of areas labeled V1 → V2 → V4 → IT (inferotemporal cortex) — two things change at each step. Receptive fields get larger (each cell looks at more of the image), and what cells respond to gets more abstract: from oriented edges, to contours and textures, to object parts, to whole objects and faces. Higher stages also gain 'invariance' — they keep recognizing an object even when it shifts position or changes size. This same feedforward-and-pooling principle shows up across the senses and is the direct architectural inspiration for deep convolutional neural networks.
depths.deep: The hierarchy trades away fine spatial detail in exchange for abstraction and invariance. It does this by alternating two kinds of stages: selectivity-increasing stages (AND-like template matching — fire only for a specific combination) and invariance-increasing stages (OR-like pooling — fire if the feature appears anywhere nearby). That is the simple-cell/complex-cell idea, generalized up the chain. Importantly, the brain's hierarchy is not a one-way street: it has abundant feedback connections carrying context and expectations back down — which is exactly what 'predictive coding' models (a later atom) try to capture.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Vision is built up in stages, like an assembly line. The first stage sees tiny edges. The next combines edges into corners and textures. The next builds shapes. The last recognizes whole objects and faces. Each stage takes the pieces found by the stage before and assembles bigger, more meaningful pieces.

### Precisely

Along the visual **ventral stream** — a chain of areas $V1 \to V2 \to V4 \to IT$ (inferotemporal cortex) — two things change at each step. **Receptive fields get larger** (each cell looks at more of the image), and responses get **more abstract**: from oriented edges, to contours and textures, to object parts, to whole objects and faces. Higher stages also gain **invariance** — they keep recognizing an object even as it shifts in position or size. The same feedforward-and-pooling principle recurs across the senses.

### Worked example

Present a face. In V1, populations of oriented simple cells fire for each local edge and its angle. In V2/V4, cells pool these into curves, corners, and texture patches that make up the face's parts. In IT, certain cells respond to a *whole face* — and keep responding when the face moves across the visual field or changes size. Move from V1 to IT and you trade *where exactly* the edges are for *what* the object is: spatial precision is exchanged for abstraction and invariance.

### Why it's true / how it works

The hierarchy alternates two complementary operations: **selectivity-increasing** stages (AND-like template matching — fire only for a specific combination) and **invariance-increasing** stages (OR-like *pooling* — fire if the feature appears anywhere nearby). That is the simple-cell/complex-cell idea generalized up the chain. Crucially the hierarchy is *not* one-way: abundant **feedback** connections carry context and expectations back down.

### Where it connects

Hierarchical processing builds on single-stage **receptive-fields** and reads out via **population-coding**. The feedback connections are the substrate of **predictive-coding** and **attention**, and the whole feedforward-pooling scheme is the direct architectural inspiration for **artificial-neural-networks** (CNNs).

### Watch out

The clean "feedforward assembly line" is a simplification. Feedback and recurrence are massive in real cortex and shape even early responses — the brain is not a pure bottom-up pipeline. Treating the ventral stream as strictly one-directional misses where context, expectation, and **perception-inference** enter.

### Worth knowing

The ventral "what" stream is only half the story: a parallel **dorsal "where/how" stream** ($V1 \to$ parietal cortex) extracts spatial location and the visual guidance of action, so the brain splits *identity* from *position* into two cooperating hierarchies. Hierarchy depth also buys **abstraction at a cost in latency** — a face-selective IT response arrives roughly $100$–$150\,\text{ms}$ after the image, the accumulated delay of each feedforward stage. And the same alternating selectivity/invariance scheme recurs *outside vision*: the auditory system builds from frequency tuning toward complex sound objects and speech, showing the principle is a general cortical strategy rather than a quirk of seeing.

atoms.title: Motor control & the motor hierarchy
atoms.summary: Movement is produced by a hierarchy from cortical planning through spinal circuits to motor units, with feedback correction throughout.

depths.eli5: Moving your body is a team effort across levels. Up top, your brain decides the goal ('reach for the cup'). Lower down, the spinal cord runs the automatic reflexes and rhythmic patterns (like the leg cycle of walking). At the bottom, muscles do the actual pulling. And all the while, feedback flows back so the system can fix small errors as the movement happens.
depths.core: The 'final common path' is the motor unit: one motor neuron plus all the muscle fibers it controls. Force is graded two ways — by recruiting more motor units and by making them fire faster. Spinal circuits handle reflexes and house 'central pattern generators,' little oscillator circuits that produce rhythmic actions like walking without needing step-by-step commands from the brain. The motor and premotor cortex plan and choose movements; the cerebellum (a structure at the back of the brain) and basal ganglia (deep brain nuclei) fine-tune timing, coordination, and which action to take. Sensory feedback and the brain's own predictions ('forward models') correct the movement while it's still in progress.
depths.deep: Control theory (the math of steering systems) fits this well. The brain runs internal 'forward models' that predict the sensory consequences of its own motor commands. That prediction lets it correct movements quickly even though real sensory feedback is delayed, and it explains why self-generated sensations feel muted — you can't tickle yourself because your brain predicted (and discounted) your own touch. At the level of populations, motor cortex activity is well described by low-dimensional dynamics — a few combined patterns that evolve over time to generate the muscle commands — a 'dynamical systems' view that has largely replaced the older idea that each neuron simply codes one movement parameter.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Moving your body is a team effort across levels. Up top, your brain decides the goal ("reach for the cup"). Lower down, the spinal cord runs automatic reflexes and rhythmic patterns (like the leg cycle of walking). At the bottom, muscles do the actual pulling. And all the while, feedback flows back so the system can fix small errors as the movement happens.

### Precisely

The **final common path** is the **motor unit**: one motor neuron plus all the muscle fibers it controls. Force is graded two ways — by **recruiting more motor units** and by making them **fire faster**. Spinal circuits handle reflexes and house **central pattern generators (CPGs)** — little oscillator circuits that produce rhythmic actions like walking without step-by-step commands. **Motor and premotor cortex** plan and select movements; the **cerebellum** and **basal ganglia** fine-tune timing, coordination, and action choice. Feedback and the brain's own predictions (**forward models**) correct movement in flight.

### Worked example

To lift a light versus heavy cup, your nervous system first recruits small, fatigue-resistant motor units, then progressively larger ones as more force is needed (the "size principle"), and also raises their firing rates. Meanwhile a **forward model** predicts the cup's expected weight and the arm's expected trajectory. If the cup is heavier than predicted, the *mismatch* between predicted and actual sensory feedback drives a fast correction — long before slow visual feedback could fully register the error.

### Why it's true / how it works

**Control theory** (the math of steering systems) fits this well. The brain runs internal **forward models** that predict the sensory consequences of its own commands, so it can correct quickly despite *delayed* real feedback — and it explains why self-generated sensations feel muted (you can't tickle yourself: your brain predicted and discounted your own touch). At the population level, motor cortex is well described by **low-dimensional dynamics** — a few combined patterns evolving over time to generate muscle commands — a "dynamical systems" view that has largely replaced "one neuron codes one parameter."

### Where it connects

Motor control reads out **population-coding** (population dynamics drive muscles) and uses the inhibitory/recurrent motifs of **neural-circuits**. Forward models connect to **perception-inference** and **predictive-coding**; action selection ties to **reinforcement-learning-brain** (basal ganglia). It is the output side decoded by **brain-computer-interfaces**.

### Watch out

Don't imagine the cortex micromanaging every muscle. Much rhythmic and reflexive movement is handled *autonomously* by spinal CPGs and reflex loops — the brain sets goals and modulates, rather than dictating each twitch. And motor cortex activity is better read as *dynamics generating commands* than as a static map of movement parameters.

### Worth knowing

The **size principle** deserves a closer look: motor units are recruited from smallest to largest as force demand grows, which automatically gives fine control at low forces (small increments) and large force when needed (big units last) — an elegant solution that falls out of motor neuron size and input resistance. The cerebellum's specific role is increasingly read as *supervised* learning of internal models: climbing-fiber "error" signals adjust cerebellar synapses so predictions improve, which is why cerebellar damage produces movements that are clumsy and poorly timed rather than weak. And the dynamical-systems view makes a concrete prediction — much of motor cortex activity during a reach reflects internal dynamics *generating* the command rather than literally representing arm position — which has reshaped how motor BCIs decode intent.

atoms.title: Hippocampus & declarative memory
atoms.summary: The hippocampus is required to form new conscious (declarative) memories and supports spatial mapping via place cells.

depths.eli5: The hippocampus is a seahorse-shaped structure deep in the brain that works like a 'save' button for new facts and events. If it's damaged, you can still recall your childhood and still learn physical skills, but you can't lay down new lasting memories of what just happened. It doubles as the brain's inner GPS, tracking where you are.
depths.core: The famous patient H.M., who had both hippocampi removed to treat epilepsy, could no longer form new declarative memories — the consciously recallable kind, covering episodic (specific events) and semantic (facts) memory — yet he kept his old memories and could still learn new motor skills. This showed the hippocampus is needed to encode new conscious memories but is not where they are permanently stored. The hippocampus also holds 'place cells' (discovered by John O'Keefe) that fire only when the animal is in a specific location, together forming a 'cognitive map'; nearby 'grid cells' in the entorhinal cortex lay down a coordinate-like grid.
depths.deep: The hippocampus rapidly binds the pieces of an experience into a single combined code, using two complementary tricks: 'pattern separation' in a region called the dentate gyrus (making similar experiences distinct so they don't blur) and 'pattern completion' in the recurrent network of region CA3 (letting a partial cue retrieve the whole memory). Both lean heavily on NMDA-receptor-dependent LTP. The same circuit 'replays' recent experience during brief bursts called sharp-wave ripples during rest and sleep — the proposed engine for copying memories into the neocortex. That place and grid cells live in the memory system hints the brain treats remembering as a kind of navigation through a represented space.

atoms.note: H.M. separates declarative (hippocampus-dependent) from procedural memory; O'Keefe and the Mosers (2014 Nobel Prize) found place and grid cells.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

The **hippocampus** is a seahorse-shaped structure deep in the brain that works like a "save" button for new facts and events. Damage it and you can still recall your childhood and still learn physical skills, but you cannot lay down new lasting memories of what just happened. It doubles as the brain's inner GPS, tracking where you are.

### Precisely

The famous patient **H.M.**, who had both hippocampi removed to treat epilepsy, could no longer form new **declarative memories** — the consciously recallable kind, covering **episodic** (specific events) and **semantic** (facts) memory — yet kept his old memories and could still learn new motor skills. This showed the hippocampus is needed to *encode* new conscious memories but is *not* where they are permanently stored. The hippocampus also holds **place cells** (O'Keefe) that fire only at specific locations, forming a **cognitive map**; nearby **grid cells** in entorhinal cortex lay down a coordinate-like grid.

### Worked example

H.M. could hold a conversation, but if you left the room and returned minutes later, he had no memory of having met you — a profound *anterograde* amnesia for new facts and events. Yet trained day after day on a mirror-drawing task, he *improved* — even while insisting each session he had never done it before. His *procedural* (skill) memory was intact while his *declarative* memory of the practice was gone. This dissociation is the cleanest evidence that the brain has multiple memory systems, with the hippocampus serving the conscious, declarative one.

### Why it's true / how it works

The hippocampus rapidly **binds** the pieces of an experience into one code using two complementary tricks: **pattern separation** in the dentate gyrus (making similar experiences distinct so they don't blur) and **pattern completion** in the recurrent CA3 network (letting a partial cue retrieve the whole memory). Both lean heavily on NMDA-dependent **ltp-ltd**. The same circuit **replays** recent experience during **sharp-wave ripples** in rest and sleep.

### Where it connects

The hippocampus is built on the plasticity of **ltp-ltd**; its replay drives **memory-consolidation**; its place/grid cells exemplify **population-coding**; and "remembering as navigation" links memory to the spatial maps of **motor-control** and to model-based **reinforcement-learning-brain**.

### Watch out

The hippocampus is *not the brain's hard drive*. It is required to *form* new declarative memories and to retrieve recent ones, but old, consolidated memories survive its loss — they have moved to the cortex. Equating "hippocampus" with "where memories are stored" gets the architecture exactly backwards.

### Worth knowing

The "memory as navigation" theme runs deep: the very same hippocampal machinery that builds spatial maps also appears to organize *non-spatial* relationships — concepts, social hierarchies, abstract task spaces — into map-like representations, suggesting the brain reuses a spatial scaffold to structure knowledge in general. Sequence is encoded too: during movement, place cells fire in ordered sequences locked to the **theta** rhythm (phase precession), and during rest those sequences *replay* compressed in time, the raw material that **memory-consolidation** ships to cortex. The Mosers' discovery of **grid cells** — neurons whose firing tiles the environment in a regular hexagonal lattice — revealed that the brain even has an intrinsic metric, a coordinate system, underlying the cognitive map.

atoms.title: Systems consolidation
atoms.summary: Memories initially dependent on the hippocampus are gradually stabilized into distributed neocortical stores, especially during sleep.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

A brand-new memory is fragile at first and leans on the hippocampus. Over days to years it gets gradually copied into the broader **cortex** (the brain's outer sheet), until it can stand on its own without the hippocampus. Sleep is when much of that copying happens — part of why sleep helps you remember.

### Precisely

**Systems consolidation** is the slow reorganization by which a memory stops depending on the hippocampus and ends up stored in distributed neocortical networks. The standard model: the hippocampus quickly binds an experience, then repeatedly **reactivates ("replays")** it — especially during **slow-wave (deep) sleep** — gradually training cortical synapses until the cortical version can stand alone. This is *distinct* from **synaptic consolidation**, the faster (hours-long) stabilization of individual synapses by new protein synthesis (covered under **ltp-ltd**).

### Worked example

Learn a list of facts today. Tonight, during slow-wave sleep, hippocampal **sharp-wave ripples** replay the day's neural patterns, time-locked to cortical **slow oscillations** and thalamic **sleep spindles**. Each replay nudges the relevant cortical synapses a little. Repeat over many nights and the memory becomes retrievable from cortex *without* needing the hippocampus — which is why a lesion that would erase a week-old memory may spare a years-old one. Disrupt that sleep and the consolidation — and the next-day recall benefit — is measurably impaired.

### Why it's true / how it works

In the **complementary learning systems** view, the hippocampus is a *fast* learner that interleaves new memories gradually into a *slow* cortical learner. Interleaving prevents new learning from overwriting old — a failure mode called **catastrophic interference**. The teaching signal is **replay** during ripples, timed to cortical slow oscillations. Consolidation is not strictly one-way: **reconsolidation** shows that recalling a memory can make it temporarily editable again before re-stabilizing — so memories can be *updated*, not just stored.

### Where it connects

Consolidation builds on **hippocampus-memory** (the fast binder) and the synaptic changes of **ltp-ltd** / **stdp**. Replay as "imagined experience" ties to **reinforcement-learning-brain** (offline training of values), and the catastrophic-interference idea was *borrowed into AI* — a direct neuroscience-to-machine-learning export.

### Watch out

Two consolidations get conflated. **Synaptic** consolidation (hours, one synapse, protein synthesis) is *not* the same as **systems** consolidation (days–years, hippocampus $\to$ cortex). And consolidation is not a permanent lock: every retrieval can reopen the memory for editing (reconsolidation), so "consolidated" does not mean "frozen forever.\"

### Worth knowing

The clearest behavioral handle on consolidation is **temporally graded retrograde amnesia**: after hippocampal damage, recent memories are lost while remote ones survive, exactly as the "gradual transfer to cortex" model predicts. Sleep's role is now well supported — targeted *cueing* during slow-wave sleep (replaying a sound or smell linked to earlier learning) measurably improves later recall, a direct causal test of the replay idea. There is an active debate, though: the *multiple-trace* / *trace-transformation* view argues that vivid episodic memories may *always* retain a hippocampal component and that only a gist-like, semanticized version becomes fully cortical — so "the hippocampus eventually becomes unnecessary" may hold for facts more than for richly re-experienced events.

atoms.title: Attention & selective processing
atoms.summary: Limited processing resources are allocated to behaviorally relevant stimuli by enhancing some signals and suppressing others.

depths.eli5: Your brain can't fully process everything hitting your senses at once, so it picks. It turns up the 'volume' on whatever matters right now and turns down everything else. That selective spotlight is attention — and it's why you can hear one person at a noisy party.
depths.core: Attention comes in two flavors: bottom-up (grabbed automatically by something salient, like a sudden flash) and top-down (aimed on purpose by your goals). Its main neural signature is gain modulation — attended stimuli make sensory neurons fire more strongly and more reliably, while competing, ignored stimuli get suppressed (an idea called 'biased competition,' where stimuli compete and attention tips the balance). Control signals come from frontoparietal networks (regions across the frontal and parietal lobes). The measurable effects are stronger firing, sharper tuning (more selective responses), and less random trial-to-trial noise for the attended feature.
depths.deep: A leading mechanistic account is 'normalization-based': attention scales the gain inside a divisive-normalization circuit (one that divides each cell's response by the total activity of its neighbors), so whether attention looks like multiplying the response or just adding to it depends on the stimulus contrast and how big the stimulus is relative to the receptive field. Attention also tunes oscillatory coherence (for example, gamma-band synchrony between areas) to route information where it's needed. In effect attention is the gatekeeper deciding which representations reach the brain's capacity-limited stage — the same stage many theories tie to conscious awareness.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Your brain cannot fully process everything hitting your senses at once, so it *picks*. It turns up the "volume" on whatever matters right now and turns down everything else. That selective spotlight is **attention** — and it is why you can follow one voice at a noisy party.

### Precisely

Attention comes in two flavors: **bottom-up** (grabbed automatically by something salient, like a sudden flash) and **top-down** (aimed on purpose by your goals). Its main neural signature is **gain modulation** — attended stimuli make sensory neurons fire *more strongly and more reliably*, while competing, ignored stimuli are *suppressed* (the **biased competition** idea, where stimuli compete and attention tips the balance). Control signals come from **frontoparietal** networks. Measurable effects: stronger firing, **sharper tuning**, and less trial-to-trial noise for the attended feature.

### Worked example

Put two stimuli inside one neuron's receptive field — a preferred red bar and a non-preferred green one. With attention spread, the cell's response is an average of the two. Now cue the animal to attend the red bar: the neuron's response shifts *toward* the response the red bar would evoke alone — as if the green competitor were partly removed. Attention "biased the competition" in favor of the attended stimulus, boosting its effective signal and suppressing the distractor.

### Why it's true / how it works

A leading mechanistic account is **normalization-based**: attention scales the gain *inside* a **divisive-normalization** circuit (one that divides each cell's response by the total activity of its neighbors). Whether attention then looks **multiplicative** (scaling the response) or **additive** (a constant boost) depends on stimulus contrast and the stimulus size relative to the receptive field. Attention also tunes **oscillatory coherence** (e.g., gamma synchrony) to route information where it is needed.

### Where it connects

Attention rests on the gain-control and inhibition motifs of **neural-circuits** and acts within **hierarchical-processing**. It is reinterpreted as **precision-weighting** in **predictive-coding**, uses the routing of **neural-oscillations**, and gates which representations reach the capacity-limited stage tied to **theories-of-consciousness**.

### Watch out

Attention is not a literal "spotlight" that simply illuminates a region — it is *competition and gain control*, so its effect on a neuron depends on what else is in the receptive field and on stimulus contrast. The same attentional manipulation can look multiplicative or additive depending on conditions, which confuses naive "attention just adds X" accounts.

### Worth knowing

Attention has a measurable *cost* and *limit*: enhancing one location or feature comes at the expense of others (the spotlight is roughly zero-sum), which is why we miss salient events when focused elsewhere — the basis of "inattentional blindness." It also operates on at least three distinct targets — **spatial** (a region), **feature-based** (a color or direction everywhere at once), and **object-based** (a whole perceptual object) — each with somewhat different neural signatures. Clinically, damage to right parietal cortex produces **hemispatial neglect**, where patients fail to attend the left side of space despite intact eyes, dramatic evidence that attention is a separable brain function whose control machinery can be lesioned independently of sensation.

atoms.title: Perception as inference
atoms.summary: Perception is the brain's best guess about the world's causes given ambiguous sensory data — unconscious inference.

depths.eli5: Your eyes and ears never give you the full, clean truth — just partial, blurry, ambiguous clues. So your brain quietly fills in the most likely story behind those clues. In other words, what you 'see' is partly an educated guess. That's exactly why optical illusions fool you: they're cases where the brain's best guess is wrong.
depths.core: Sensory input doesn't pin down the world uniquely — this is the 'inverse problem': many different real scenes can produce the very same image on your retina (for example, a small near object and a large far one). So the brain has to infer the likely cause using prior knowledge — what Hermann von Helmholtz called 'unconscious inference.' A striking demonstration is cue combination: when people judge something using both sight and touch, they weight each sense by how reliable it is, almost exactly as an ideal statistical observer would — evidence that the brain effectively computes with probabilities.
depths.deep: Formally, perception approximates Bayesian inference: you combine the 'likelihood' (how well the current sensory evidence fits each possible cause) with a 'prior' (your expectations and the statistics of natural scenes) to land on the most probable cause — the 'posterior.' Under this view, illusions, flip-flopping (bistable) percepts, and context effects aren't malfunctions; they're the fingerprints of priors and of competing hypotheses fighting it out. This 'Bayesian brain' framing is the bridge from earlier atoms (receptive fields, population codes) to predictive coding and to theories of what we consciously experience.
